By a correspondence referenced No. 036/09/AMB dated 09 February 2009, the Republic of Algeria transmitted to the Secretariat of the Commission its observations on the admissibility of the Communication submitted by the CFDA.

In response to the observations submitted by the Algerian government, the CFDA, with the support of the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), sent to the African Commission its observations through a document dated 3 April 2009.

At its 47th Ordinary Session held from 12 to 26 May 2010, the Commission considered the Communication and declared it admissible. The decision was notified to the parties by letter and note verbale of 01 July 2010 by which the Secretariat had also invited the Respondent State to submit its arguments on the merits of the Communication.
Notes verbales serving as reminders were sent to the Respondent State notably on 8 June 2011, 12 June 2012 and 21 August 2012, requesting it to submit its arguments on the merits.
On 21 September 2012, the Secretariat received a request for an extension of time limits so that the Respondent State could produce its arguments on the merits of the case.

On 25 September 2012, the Secretariat of the Commission acknowledged receipt of the State's request and granted an extension of time limits in accordance with Rule 113(2) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure.

On 05 October 2012, the Secretariat received from the Respondent State a motion for review of the decision on the admissibility of the Communication. The Secretariat acknowledged receipt on 14 November 2012 and transmitted it the same day to the Complainant for its observations.
On 05 February 2013, the Complainant sent its observations on the motion for review submitted by the Respondent State.
During its 13th Extraordinary Session held from 18 to 25 February 2013 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission considered the Respondent State's motion for review and declared it inadmissible.
On 05 March 2013, the Secretariat of the Commission communicated to the parties the decision taken by the African Commission and invited the Complainant to submit its observations on the merits.

On 25 September 2013, the Secretariat received the Complainant's observations on the merits. It acknowledged receipt on 3 October 2013 and transmitted them the same day to the Respondent State for its observations.
By note verbale of 24 February 2014, the Respondent State informed the Commission that its observations on the merits were being prepared.

By note verbale of 3 April 2014, which reached the Secretariat on 6 April 2014, the Respondent State sent its observations on the merits of the communication. The Secretariat acknowledged receipt on 11 April 2014 and informed it that its observations would be presented to the Commission for a decision as to the admission of its arguments submitted out of time.

At its 16th Extraordinary Session held from 20 to 29 July 2014 in Kigali, Rwanda, the Commission considered the Communication and decided, in the interest of the proper administration of justice, to admit the Respondent State's observations on the merits.

By note verbale of 15 August 2014, the Secretariat notified the parties of the Commission's decision to admit the Respondent State's observations. It also transmitted the said observations to the Complainant on the same date and invited it to submit its reply brief within one month, in accordance with Rule 108(2) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure.
On 11 September 2014, the Secretariat received from the Complainant its reply brief to the Respondent State's observations and acknowledged receipt on 18 September 2014.

In its brief, the Complainant maintains that throughout more than ten (10) years of proceedings, the father and the mother of the disappeared person, Mahmoud Benidir and Houria Berkane, have vainly seized various administrative and judicial authorities of their country so that light may be shed on the fate of their son. A reminder of the chronology of the various administrative and judicial remedies pursued by the claimant party proves necessary in order to understand its claims.

According to the Complainant, on the administrative level, a first remedy was initially pursued by a written letter dated 29 August 1996 addressed to the President of the National Observatory of Human Rights (ONDH) in which Mahmoud Benidir protests against the arbitrary nature of his son's arrest. On 27 April 1999, the ONDH responds to his request by indicating to the person concerned that his son was not arrested by the security services, nor sought by them; but that he was rather arrested by an unknown armed group. This would explain the unsuccessful searches. This response is, however, deemed insufficient given that the claimant party alleges that the witnesses present at the arrest of Ali Benidir identified the "patriots" as the perpetrators.
Then, on 19 October 1997, Mahmoud Benidir wrote a letter to the then President of the Algerian Republic, Mr Lamine Zeroual, concerning the fate of his son.

Additionally, on 21 January 2003, a letter was addressed by Mr Mahmoud Benidir to the Office of the Prime Minister demanding that light be shed on the fate of his son. In its reply dated 17 February 2003, the Office of the Prime Minister informs Mr Mahmoud Benidir that his request has been transferred to the Ministry of Justice.
Also, on 22 February 2006, Mahmoud sent a correspondence to the Minister of the Interior and to the Minister of Justice regarding the fate of his son.
On the other hand, on 22 February 2006, Houria Berkane also wrote to the Minister of Justice to request that searches be conducted to find her disappeared son.

Finally, on 4 April 2006, Houria Berkane wrote to the office of the Prime Minister in order to obtain information on her disappeared son. The office of the Prime Minister replied to her by a letter dated 18 April 2006 notifying her that her request had been transferred to the National Consultative Commission for the Promotion and Protection of Human Rights (replacing the ONDH).

On the judicial level, on 16 September 1996, Mahmoud Benedir files a first complaint with the Hussein Dey Court against the "patriots" identified as the perpetrators of the abduction of his son. Following this complaint, the person concerned is summoned twice to the Ain Naadja gendarmerie, on 25 May 1997 and on 27 August 1998.
Then, on 26 May 1998, the family's appointed lawyer, Counsel Mohamed Tahri, seizes the Public Prosecutor at the Hussein Dey Court requesting him to proceed with the questioning of the "patriots".

Also, on 1 September 1999, Mahmoud Benidir is summoned by the examining magistrate of the Hussein Dey Court where he will be questioned twice. Subsequently, on 27 September of the same year, Mahmoud Benidir receives a notification from the Hussein Dey Court indicating to him that the investigation of the case concerning his son is transferred to the Military Court of Blida on the ground that the "patriots" implicated fall under the military jurisdiction of Blida. It follows that the said "patriots" implicated are summoned by the military court; however, only their leader will answer the summons. During his hearing, the latter denies any involvement in the abduction of Ali Benidir. The military court never rendered a decision; Mr Mahmoud Benidir sent two letters which remained unanswered.

Moreover, in the context of an investigation opened by the examining magistrate of the Hussein Dey Court in 2000, two neighbours of the Benidir family and witnesses to the abduction of Ali Benidir, Boualem Harkas and Ali Renane, will be summoned respectively on 23 April 2003 and 11 March 2006. The father of the disappeared person is also summoned on 15 April 2003.

In addition, on 19 March 2005, Mahmoud Benidir will receive a notification in which the Attorney General of the Court of Algiers specifies that he has decided to follow the case concerning the abduction of Ali Benidir. Another letter dated 12 July 2005 tells him not to carry out his own searches.

On 31 December 2005, Mahmoud Benidir receives a letter from the Prosecutor at the Hussein Dey Court informing him that the case of the disappearance of his son finally falls within the civil courts according to Article 141 of the law on civil procedures and Article 3 of the Family Code.

Thus, on 16 April 2006, two months after the entry into force of the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation (presidential decree No. 05-278 of 14 August 2005) and of its implementing texts, notably Ordinance No. 06-01 of 27 February 2006 implementing the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation (Ordinance No. 06-01), a judgment of disappearance concerning Ali Benidir is pronounced by the Civil Affairs Chamber of the Hussein Dey Court and on 18 April 2006, the examining magistrate finally issues an order of non-suit. Mr Mahmoud Benidir appeals this order on 29 April 2006. The Deputy Attorney General of the Republic at the Hussein Dey Court informs him that his appeal will be examined by the indictment chamber of the court.

The appeal against the order lodged by Mahmoud Benidir will be examined on 27 June 2006 by the Indictment Chamber of the Hussein Dey Court. The latter confirms the order of non-suit pronounced a few months earlier by the examining magistrate.

According to the author of the Communication, the excessive delays and the successive non-suits resulting from the various investigation procedures manifestly demonstrate the lack of will of the Algerian authorities to rule on the case of the human rights violations alleged by the Benidir family concerning the disappearance of their son. Consequently, the claimant party maintains that the remedies thus used were neither available nor effective.

The Complainant also maintains that following the complaints addressed to him by the parents of the disappeared Ali Benidir, the Public Prosecutor was seized of the case concerning his disappearance. The authors of the Communication conclude from this that the action of the Public Prosecutor's Office was set in motion and followed by the opening of a judicial investigation. And therefore, consequently, the filing of a complaint with constitution as civil party before the examining magistrate was not necessary in this case and cannot be considered an effective remedy on the same facts.

In addition, the claimant party develops the argument that the adoption by referendum, on 29 September 2005, of the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation as well as its implementing texts henceforth makes impossible any existence of effective, useful and available local remedies for the families of victims of enforced disappearances. This assessment is mainly based on Article 45 of Ordinance No. 06-01 which provides that "no proceedings may be brought, individually or collectively, against members of any component of the defence and security forces of the Republic, for actions undertaken with a view to protecting persons and preserving the institutions of the People's Democratic Republic of Algeria. Any denunciation or complaint must be declared inadmissible by the competent judicial authority".
The Complainant concludes that the obligation of prior exhaustion of local remedies cannot therefore apply to the present Communication.

The Respondent State maintains that the alleged victims did not truly initiate and conduct judicial proceedings to their conclusion by exercising the remedies available on appeal and in cassation as provided for by the Code of Criminal Procedure in its Articles 72 and 73. The Respondent State explains that, contrary to the assertions of the author of the Communication, the Algerian judicial system applies the principle according to which the Public Prosecutor has discretion as to prosecution, that is to say that he may set the public action in motion and, otherwise, to remedy the default or inaction of the Public Prosecutor's Office, seizure by way of a complaint with constitution as civil party suffices to trigger, ipso facto, the public action, which would have the effect of obliging the examining magistrate to investigate the facts contained in the complaint, even if the prosecution office has decided otherwise.

Thus, the Respondent State considers that the applicants cannot invoke the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation and its implementing texts to exempt themselves from not having initiated the available judicial proceedings, constituting local remedies.

Finally, it is useful to mention the preliminary observations made by the Respondent State relating to the admissibility of the Communication. According to the latter, it is not appropriate for the African Commission to proceed with the examination of this type of Communications on the basis of individual treatment. The State recalls in its brief on admissibility the domestic socio-political and security context in Algeria during the 1990s, a period corresponding to the occurrence of the dispute brought before the African Commission.

The Respondent State considers that efforts at the national level are being made to address the dramatic file of the "disappeared", efforts sanctioned by the implementation of the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation. 24th Extraordinary Session, 30 July to 8 August 2018

Article 56 of the African Charter defines the admissibility conditions applicable to communications other than inter-State ones. To be declared admissible, and according to the terms of the said article, communications thus submitted must: 1) Indicate their authors even if the latter requests anonymity; 2) Be compatible with the Charter of the Organization of African Unity or with the present Charter; 3) Not contain any disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned and its institutions or the OAU; 4) Not be based exclusively on news disseminated through the mass media; 5) Be sent after exhausting local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged; 6) Be submitted within a reasonable period from the time local remedies are exhausted or from the date the Commission is seized with the matter; 7) Not deal with cases which have been settled by these States involved in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, or the Charter of the Organization of African Unity or the provisions of the present Charter.

In the present communication, the main point of discord between the parties regarding the admissibility of the communication relates to the applicability of the condition of exhaustion of local remedies; the six (6) other admissibility conditions of a Communication under the African Charter not being the subject of any dispute. However, the African Commission considers it necessary to proceed with a point-by-point examination of all the requirements of Article 56 of the African Charter.

On the first ground drawn from Article 56(1), it emerges that the identity of the author of the Communication as well as those of the victims has been documented. The African Commission concludes from this that this requirement is fulfilled.

On the 2nd ground drawn from Article 56(2), the compatibility of the present Communication with the African Charter is beyond doubt. Indeed, the complaint alleges the violation of Articles 5, 6, 7(1) of the African Charter by the People's Democratic Republic of Algeria, a State that ratified the said Charter on 1 March 1987. Also, the allegations contained in the complaint post-date the ratification of the African Charter by the State party. Thus, the African Commission deduces from this that this requirement is satisfied.

On the 3rd ground drawn from Article 56(3), the African Commission analysed the content of the complaint and deduced that it is drafted in terms that are in no way disparaging or insulting. It follows that this Communication meets the above-mentioned requirement.

On the 4th ground drawn from Article 56(4), the examination of the information contained in the present Communication shows that it does not represent a mere grouping of news conveyed by the mass media. On the very contrary, the complaint is based on court documents and exchanges of administrative correspondence to establish the culpability of the Algerian Government. Thus, the African Commission considers that this requirement is fulfilled.

On the 5th ground drawn from Article 56(5), the rule of exhaustion of local remedies prescribed in Article 56, paragraph 5 of the African Charter is underpinned by the logic of sparing the local authorities, and more specifically the national courts, the possibility of remedying by themselves the alleged violations. The Commission notes, however, that the local remedies whose exhaustion is thus required must meet the criteria of availability, effectiveness and sufficiency enshrined in the case of Jawara v. The Gambia. In the leading decision, the Commission elaborated on the meaning of these criteria by deciding that a remedy is considered available when it can be pursued without impediment by the petitioner, that it is effective if it offers a prospect of success and that it is sufficient when it is capable of giving satisfaction to the complainant and redressing the alleged violation.

On the question of the nature of the remedy that the complainant must attempt to exhaust under Article 56(5) of the African Charter, the Commission has also ruled on it in its precedents. The principle is that the remedies whose exhaustion is required are primarily of a judicial nature as enshrined in the case of Cudjoe v. Ghana.

In the present Communication, if the analysis of the arguments of the respondent party tends to support that local remedies exist, it remains true that the effectiveness of the said remedies remains improbable. Indeed, proof of the effectiveness of such remedies could not be clearly established by the Respondent State, but also it does not match the possibility offered to the victim of finding redress before the national courts. If the Algerian authorities put forward the possibility offered to the victim of having recourse to the procedure and of initiating the steps provided for by the implementing texts of the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation, it should nevertheless be noted that this possibility is not stricto sensu a judicial remedy.

On the one hand, the African Commission notes that from the date of seizure of the local judicial bodies until the day of its seizure more than ten (10) years ago, the various steps undertaken by the Benidir family to establish the truth about the fate of their disappeared son found no favourable forum.

On the other hand, the African Commission considers that the overall treatment and handling of the file of the disappeared, the object of the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation, cannot singularly deprive a victim of his right to justice or of asserting his right to reparation before a competent international body.

That consequently, if it is possible that local remedies are available, the time elapsed attests to their manifestly abnormal prolongation and thus anticipates their ineffectiveness with regard to the victim's chance of finding redress. Consequently, the African Commission considers that this requirement is satisfied.

On the 6th ground drawn from Article 56(6), the African Commission notes that the Complaint was received by the Secretariat on 17 October 2007, a little more than one year after the pronouncement of the order of non-suit relating to the disappearance of Ali Benidir on 27 June 2006 by the Indictment Chamber of the Hussein Dey Court. Thus, basing itself on the nature of the case presented before it, the African Commission considers that the Complainant's application was submitted within a reasonable period, thus satisfying this condition.

Finally, under the provisions of Article 56(7), the Communication must not deal with matters which have been settled in accordance with the principles of the Charter of the United Nations, the Constitutive Act of the African Union or the African Charter. The Commission recalls that these provisions require the Communication to respect the principles of res judicata or authority of the matter judged; of non-lis pendens and of non bis in idem.

In the present case, the Commission notes that, apart from the actions undertaken before the national courts, the Complainant maintains that the Ali Benidir case was transmitted to the Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances (the Working Group) which concluded on 19 October 1998 that this disappearance had not been clarified.

While recognising the relevance and usefulness of the procedures conducted by the Working Group in this case, the Commission refers to its jurisprudence cited supra, to recall the meaning of the requirement of res judicata made in Article 56(7) of the African Charter. In this regard, the Commission reiterates that the decisions of United Nations Treaty Bodies or of any other international bodies having a mandate to hear complaints concerning human rights violations may constitute res judicata, provided that the said bodies apply principles consistent with those prescribed in Article 56(7) of the African Charter.

The Commission notes that the Working Group is not a United Nations treaty body any more than it applies the principles laid down in Article 56(7) of the African Charter. Moreover, the case is not pending before any other body referred to in the provisions of the same article. Finally, and consequently, there is no reason to fear that the Respondent State could be the subject of double prosecution let alone of a conviction in this same case. The Commission concludes from this that the Communication respects the condition examined.
In sum, the Commission finds that the Communication complies with all the requirements of Article 56 of the African Charter and that it should therefore be declared admissible.

In view of the facts and arguments presented by the parties, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights declares the present Communication admissible in accordance with the provisions of Article 56 of the African Charter.

In its brief for the motion for review, the Respondent State states that it recently obtained factual and procedural elements, either official confirmations or written and material evidence from the administrations concerned.

On the one hand, the Respondent State relies on Rule 117.2 of the Commission's Rules of Procedure relating to the question of "additional information" in the procedure aimed at determining admissibility.

On the other hand, the Respondent State points out the unity of the procedure for examining a Communication both in its part relating to admissibility and in its part relating to the merits, which implies, according to the State, that the entire file of the present Communication remains open.

The Respondent State alleges the lis pendens of the Benidir Ali case before the Working Group on Enforced Disappearances of the United Nations Human Rights Council. It maintains, moreover, that this case is part of the 2704 cases of allegations of disappearance that allegedly occurred in Algeria.

According to the Respondent State, the Benidir Ali case is listed on the list of the Working Group on Enforced Disappearances under No. 3402 and appears on the reconciliation statement drawn up by the Algerian authorities under number 263 and is mentioned as "disappeared, declared deceased by the rightful claimants who have been compensated".

The Respondent State maintains that exchanges between the State and the Working Group on Enforced Disappearances are still ongoing with a view to reaching either decisions of closure or decisions of clarification of the cases submitted. Consequently, the Respondent State affirms that the Benidir Ali case has not yet been the subject of a final decision and concludes that the Commission should declare the Communication inadmissible.

In its brief on the review, the Respondent State affirms that Mrs Boudahane Nadjat, wife of Benidir Ali, requested and obtained a judgment declaring the death of her husband Benedir Ali and the authorisation to transcribe the death in the civil status registers. It maintains, moreover, that having become final, this judgment was rendered on the basis of the provisions of the Code of Status relating to absence and disappearance, and of Articles 27 to 30 of Ordinance No. 06/01.

The Respondent State maintains that on 27 June 2006, the Indictment Chamber of the Court of Algiers rendered a judgment by which it confirms the examining magistrate's order of non-suit, the judicial investigation having failed to gather sufficient evidence or even concordant elements as to the responsibility of the two persons implicated in the abduction of the victim. In the State's view, the civil party did not see fit to lodge an appeal in cassation before the Supreme Court against the judgment of the Indictment Chamber although the law gave it the option of using this remedy.

The Respondent State maintains that since February 2007 the victims have benefited from compensation in the form of a monthly pension distributed between the mother Berkane Houria, the widow Boudahane Nadjat and the daughter Benidir Anfal; the father, Benedir Mahmoud having died in 2008. It therefore considers that the Benedir Ali case was the subject of an amicable settlement within the framework of a consensual and legal treatment with all of his rightful claimants; his mother, his wife and his daughter.

In view of these elements, the Respondent State considers that Ms Yous Nassera, acting on behalf of the association "Collective of Families of the Disappeared in Algeria", a French NGO based in Paris, cannot claim to legally represent the members of a family who are not fully and directly involved in the entire settlement mechanism of this case brought about by the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation.

In the view of the Respondent State, neither Ms Yous Nassera, nor the Collective of Families of the Disappeared can produce a special power of attorney emanating from the rightful claimants of Benidir Ali, conferring on them the prerogative to represent them and to submit in their name and on their behalf a communication before the Commission. Consequently, Ms Yous Nassera and the Collective of Families of the Disappeared in Algeria cannot in any capacity, express or tacit, claim to represent them before the African Commission within the framework of a communication procedure.

In light of the grounds thus invoked, the Algerian State requests the Commission to: - Find that Communication No. 348/07 - Collective of Families of the Disappeared v. Algeria, concerns a case which is already before a settlement mechanism of the United Nations Human Rights Council. - Find that at the domestic level, the Benidir Ali case was the subject of an amicable settlement with the rightful claimants within the framework of the provisions of the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation who never saw fit to lodge an appeal in cassation before the Supreme Court. - Find that the Collective of Families of the Disappeared in Algeria and Ms Yous Nassera have no legal standing to claim to represent the rightful claimants of Benidir Ali with a view to submitting and pursuing in their name a communication under Article 55 of the African Charter. - Find that this NGO which has set itself up as a source of communication lacks objectivity and sincerity in all its actions aimed exclusively at Algeria. - Declare communication No. 348/07, Collective of Families of the Disappeared v. Algeria inadmissible.

The Complainant submits to the Commission two observations relating, on the one hand, to the review of a decision on admissibility and, on the other hand, to the arguments raised by the Respondent State.

The Complainant maintains that the Respondent State's request for review is devoid of any legal basis. He maintains that the provision to which the Respondent State refers, that is Rule 117(2) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure, no longer exists. Even if it still existed, the Complainant considers that the State has misinterpreted it.

According to the Complainant, this article provided that "a Communication may be declared admissible only on condition that the State party concerned has had the opportunity to submit information or observations in accordance with paragraph 1 of this article". The Complainant finds that this article provides for no review procedure, which is provided for only in Rule 111 of the Commission's Rules of Procedure, but only on the merits.

The Complainant concludes on this point that no review procedure on the admissibility of a Communication is provided for either in the African Charter or in the Commission's Rules of Procedure and, therefore, requests the Commission to reject the Respondent State's request without examining its arguments relating to the substance of the review.

On the Respondent State's arguments, the Complainant maintains that the State has not proven the existence of a new fact, a compelling reason or a situation that the Commission could deem appropriate or that could justify the review of the Communication, in a spirit of fairness, justice, and respect for human and peoples' rights.

On the lis pendens of the Benidir Ali case before the Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances of the United Nations Human Rights Council, the Complainant recalls that the extra-conventional procedures or mechanisms set up by the Commission (or Council) on Human Rights, whose mandate consists in examining and publicly reporting on the human rights situation in a particular country, do not generally fall within an international procedure of investigation or settlement within the meaning of Rule 93.2 of the Commission's Rules of Procedure.

The Complainant puts forward that the Respondent State had raised no objection although it had been invited to do so by the Commission. Therefore, the Complainant considers that the Commission has already examined this question and considered that the Communication was admissible on this point.

On the lack of legal standing of Ms Yous Nassera of the CFDA, the Complainant maintains that these are not new facts because, according to him, the Respondent State already had the opportunity to raise it in its statement of defence of 09 February 2009. The Complainant affirms that he has the necessary legal standing as he received a representation mandate from the victims.

The Complainant therefore requests the Commission to reject the Respondent State's request without examining the arguments put forward for lack of legal basis. In the event that the Commission nevertheless decides to examine the Respondent State's arguments, the Complainant requests that they be rejected because they are unfounded.

The Commission recalls that it declared the communication admissible at its 47th Ordinary Session held in Banjul, The Gambia, from 12 to 26 May 2010. The parties were informed thereof on 1 July 2010. On 05 October 2012, the Respondent State submitted a motion for review of the Commission's decision on admissibility.

It is important to note that the Commission's Rules of Procedure as they stand provide for review only in Rule 111 relating to a decision rendered on the merits. With respect to decisions rendered on admissibility, only a communication declared inadmissible may be reconsidered at a later date if the Commission receives a written request from the author on the basis of new elements in accordance with the provisions of Rule 107(4) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure.
In light of its Rules of Procedure, the Commission therefore cannot reconsider its decision on a Communication that it has already declared admissible.
From the foregoing, the Commission declares the Respondent State's request inadmissible and invites it to submit its observations on the merits.

The Complainant alleges the violation by the Respondent State of several provisions of the African Charter on account of its failures to conduct serious investigations making it possible to prosecute the culprits of the enforced disappearance of Ali Benidir and to determine the fate of the latter. The Complainant adds that Ordinance No. 06-01 prevents any judicial step, in that the provisions of its Article 45 prohibit recourse to justice to shed light on enforced disappearances, requiring the competent judicial authorities to declare any denunciation or complaint inadmissible.

The Complainant alleges that the Respondent State violated the general obligations incumbent on the State under Article 1 as well as the rights protected by Articles 4, 5, 6, 7(1) and 9(2) of the African Charter.

The complainant alleges that the Respondent State violated the general obligations incumbent on it under Article 1 which establishes a general obligation for States parties. He indicates that the recognition of human rights implies the commitment to create the conditions necessary for the exercise of these rights to be made possible.
The Complainant indicates that the failure to comply with this obligation, by action or omission of any of the powers of the State, engages the international responsibility of the latter.

The Complainant further indicates that Article 1 imposes a positive but also a negative obligation, in that States parties cannot adopt legislative measures contrary to the African Charter. Thus the fact for a State of adopting provisions not in conformity with the Charter constitutes in itself a violation of the obligations provided for in Article 1.

The Complainant alleges that Ali Benidir has been disappeared since his arrest by the patriots, on 29 August 1996. Following his arrest, Ali Benidir's parents seized the Algerian courts, cooperating fully with them by attending the various summonses and providing all useful information with a view to discovering the truth about the fate of Ali Benidir. He deplores that at the end of more than seventeen years of proceedings, the fate of Ali Benidir has still not been clarified and that his prolonged absence suggests that he lost his life in incommunicado detention, thus entailing a high risk of violation of the right to life.

The Complainant affirms that the perpetrators of the abduction, although known to the Algerian authorities and identified by two witnesses, were never prosecuted. Mahmoud Benidir, father of Ali Benidir, states that he contacted a lawyer who seized the Public Prosecutor of Hussein Dey in May 1998. The family's lawyer clearly indicated, in his letter of seizure, the identity of the patriots responsible for the arrest of Ali Benidir, who were identified by two witnesses.

In support of his claims, the Complainant cites the jurisprudence of the United Nations Human Rights Committee to support the violation of the right to life which considers that "deprivation of liberty, followed by a refusal to acknowledge it or by concealment of the fate of the disappeared person or of his whereabouts, removes that person from the protection of the law and regularly exposes him to a serious risk to his life for which the State must be held accountable". He also cites the Commission's jurisprudence in which the African Commission considered that enforced disappearance constitutes a violation of the right to physical and moral integrity. He adds that Article 4 also implies a duty of protection of the State. The Complainant indicates to that effect that even if the death of Ali Benidir is not established, the mere risk or danger for persons of losing their lives constitutes sufficient ground to conclude that there has been a violation of the right to life.

The Complainant alleges that acts of physical torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment were allegedly inflicted on Ali Benidir during the detention following his first arrest of 17 April 1995. In support of such an allegation, the Complainant indicates that during the ten days of detention, Ali Benidir allegedly suffered, during the interrogation on his links with the FIS (Islamic Salvation Front), acts of torture such as the rag torture, beating with truncheons, his genitals being tied with a wire to prevent him from urinating, detention in a cell devoid of everything, flooded with water, where he had to sleep on the bare floor, naked and without a blanket.

The Complainant further alleges that Ali Benidir's wife (Boudahane Nadjat) and his mother (Houria Berkane) also suffered moral torture in that the disappearance of Mr Benidir, since his arrest on 29 August 1996 by the patriots, has caused anguish and distress among his relatives.

The Complainant cites a jurisprudence of the United Nations Human Rights Committee with regard to Algeria according to which the obligation for the family to declare the disappeared person dead in order to receive compensation, although there is no certainty and the investigation is still ongoing, amounts to a harmful procedure and constitutes a violation of Article 2 §3, read in conjunction with Articles 6, 7 and 9 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, and therefore constitutes cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment with regard to the family.

The Complainant also relies on a dissenting opinion of Mr Fabian Salvioli in Communication Rizvanovic v. Bosnia and Herzegovina, decided by the Human Rights Committee on 21 March 2014. Mr Fabian Salvioli considers that the State's obligation to investigate human rights violations and to prosecute their perpetrators constitutes an obligation of means. By contrast, in matters of enforced disappearance, the State has an obligation of result with regard to the victim's family, namely to locate the disappeared person or to find his body. Otherwise, he considers that the inhuman and cruel treatment is continuous for the family of the disappeared person who is unaware of the truth about his fate.

The complainant also alleges the violation of the right to respect for human dignity and of the right to recognition of the legal status of Ali Benidir. Regarding the alleged violation of the right to respect for the dignity inherent in the human being, the Complainant cites the Commission's jurisprudence in the case Mouvement Burkinabé des droits de l'homme et des peuples v. Burkina Faso and indicates that enforced disappearance constitutes by its very nature a negation of the right to respect for human dignity. The Complainant alleges that by making Ali BENIDIR disappear and by conducting no serious investigation into his disappearance, the Algerian authorities failed in their obligation to respect and ensure respect for the rights of a person deprived of liberty to be treated with humanity and with respect for the dignity inherent in the human being.

Concerning the right to recognition of legal status, the Complainant states that an enforced disappearance constitutes a refusal to recognise the legal status of the victim. According to the Complainant, by keeping Ali BENIDIR in detention without acknowledging it, the Algerian authorities consequently removed him from the protection of the law and deprived him of his right to recognition of his legal status, in violation of Article 5 of the African Charter.

The Complainant alleges that Ali Benidir was arrested on 29 August 1996 by "Patriots" and has not been seen again by his family. Neither his arrest nor his detention were legally motivated and recorded in any official register. The Complainant maintains that the investigations lacked the effective and efficient character required in these circumstances, and the official authorities persist in concealing the fate that was reserved for him. For the Complainant, this arrest and the secrecy surrounding his detention constitute arbitrary detention under Article 6 of the African Charter.

The Complainant refers to the Commission's jurisprudence which considers that the enforced disappearance of a person is a violation of Article 6 as well as the jurisprudence of the United Nations Human Rights Committee which also considers that the incommunicado detention of a person constitutes a violation of Article 9 of the Covenant which enshrines the right to liberty and security of person.

The Complainant alleges that the right to a judicial remedy was violated not only with regard to Ali Benidir but also with regard to his mother Houria Berkane, wife of Benidir. He maintains that the Benidir family approached all the competent authorities of the Algerian State and exhausted all local remedies both before the judicial and administrative authorities. The Complainant further maintains that all the steps proved useless insofar as they yielded no result.

The Complainant further alleges that following the promulgation of Ordinance No. 06-01, any denunciation or complaint by the Benidir family will be declared inadmissible. He indicates that Article 45 of Ordinance No. 06-01 prohibits recourse to justice to shed light on the most serious crimes such as enforced disappearances, requiring the competent judicial authorities to declare any denunciation or complaint inadmissible.

The Complainant affirms that the entry into force of Ordinance No. 06-01 prevents any judicial action against State agents. Indeed, under Article 45 of this ordinance: "No proceedings may be brought, individually or collectively against members of any component of the defence and security forces of the Republic [...]". He continues that Article 46 of Ordinance No. 06-01 goes further in that it provides for a prison sentence of three to five years and a fine of 250,000 DA to 500,000 DA for: "anyone who, by his statements, writings or any other act, uses or instrumentalises the wounds of the national tragedy, to undermine the institutions of the People's Democratic Republic of Algeria, weaken the State, harm the honourability of its agents who have served it with dignity, or tarnish the image of Algeria internationally. Criminal proceedings are initiated ex officio by the public prosecutor's office. In the event of a repeat offence, the penalty provided for in this article is doubled".

According to the Complainant, all the steps undertaken by the parents of Ali Benidir after the entry into force of Ordinance No. 06-01 remained in vain. Indeed, the attorney general of the Hussein Dey court issued an order of non-suit on 18 April 2006. According to the Complainant, Ordinance No. 06-01 is merely a legal consecration of an already widespread practice in that the Algerian authorities refuse to shed light on the fate of the disappeared and conduct no impartial and thorough investigation.

The Complainant reports that Article 46 of Ordinance No. 06-01 provides for imprisonment and a fine for anyone who "uses or instrumentalises the wounds of the national tragedy, to undermine the institutions of the People's Democratic Republic of Algeria, weaken the State, harm the honourability of its agents who have served it with dignity, or tarnish the image of Algeria internationally".

He indicates that by virtue of this article, the family is prevented from communicating about their grief and distress caused by the disappearance of their son. Thus, Houria Berkane, wife of Benidir, risks imprisonment of three to five years and a fine of 250,000 DA to 500,000 DA each time she speaks of her distress or mobilises in a peaceful gathering in favour of truth and justice. This constitutes a direct violation of the freedom of expression provided for in Article 9 of the African Charter.

The Complainant further cites the concluding observations of the United Nations Human Rights Committee in the context of the examination of Algeria's report in 2007, which recommends that the State party "repeal any provision of Ordinance No. 06/01 implementing the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation, [...] which undermines freedom of expression as well as the right of every person to have access to an effective remedy against human rights violations, both at the national and international level".

In addition to the violation of the rights guaranteed in Articles 1, 4, 5, 6, 7(1) and 9(2) of the Charter, the Complainant alleges the violation of Article 2 § 3 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and Articles 13, 14 and 19 of the Declaration of 18 December 1992 on the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance.

In its brief on the merits, the Respondent State once again raises the objection relating to the inadmissibility of the case for three reasons. Firstly, it maintains that the Complainant did not exhaust local remedies and explains that the alleged facts were brought to the attention of the Algerian justice system by the father of the victim, Mr Mahmoud Benidir, who filed a complaint for abduction before the Hussein Dey court.

The Respondent State puts forward that all the investigations undertaken did not convince the examining magistrate as to the merit of the accusations; which led the magistrate to issue an order of non-suit which, appealed by the complainant, was confirmed by the Indictment Chamber of the Court of Algiers for absence of sufficient elements in the procedural file making it possible to engage the responsibility of the persons suspected by the civil party.

The Respondent State maintains that local remedies were not exhausted because the civil party did not use another remedy offered by law, namely, the appeal in cassation before the Supreme Court. The Respondent State considers the attitude of renouncing the use of a remedy offered by law as an acceptance of the court's decision.

The Respondent State concludes that the remedies recognised by law not having been exhausted in their entirety, the complainant cannot bring the complaint before the Commission, on pain of violating the principle by virtue of which an international mechanism cannot rule on a case which has not been brought before the national courts and for which all remedies have not been exhausted.

Secondly, the Respondent State puts forward the lis pendens of the Benidir Ali case before the Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances (WGEID). It affirms that the WGEID of the United Nations Human Rights Council remains seized of the Benidir Ali case, which is part of the allegations of disappearances that occurred in Algeria, appearing in the list in the WGEID's annual report, under No. 3402.

For the Respondent State, the allegations of disappearances are examined within the framework of the WGEID's procedures for a reconciliation of the official lists of victims of the national tragedy, presented by the Algerian Government, which were the subject of a settlement under the provisions of the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation. The Benidir case is listed under No. 263, entered as "disappeared, declared deceased by the rightful claimants who have been compensated".

The Respondent State affirms that exchanges of correspondence, contacts and formal meetings continue between the representatives of the Algerian Government and the members of the WGEID, on the basis of the working rules and procedures of this body, with a view to reaching either decisions of closure or clarification of the cases submitted.

Thirdly, the Respondent State challenges the mandate of Ms Yous Nassera to act on behalf of the rightful claimants. The Respondent State considers that Ms Yous Nassera, acting on behalf of the association "Collective of Families of the Disappeared in Algeria", an NGO under French law based in Paris, cannot claim to legally represent the members of a family which has benefited from the mechanism for the care of the families of victims put in place in application of the provisions of the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation.

The Respondent State attests that the rightful claimants of the disappeared Benidir Ali, declared deceased, a victim of the national tragedy, have benefited since February 2007 from compensation in the form of a monthly pension distributed between the mother Berkane Houria, the widow Boudahane Nadjat and the daughter Benidir Anfal; the father, Benidir Mahmoud, having died in 2008. It further maintains that the rightful claimants of Benidir Ali (his mother, his wife and his daughter) voluntarily adhered to the care provided for by the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation, within the framework of the political settlement of the national tragedy, adopted by referendum.

Therefore, the Respondent State considers that neither Ms Yous Nassera, nor the Collective of Families of the Disappeared, can rely on any duly established mandate of representation to act or to submit in the name and on behalf of the rightful claimants of Benidir Ali a communication before the African Commission or any other body. For all these reasons, the Respondent State requests the Commission to review its decision and to declare the present Communication inadmissible.

Regarding the arguments on the merits of the Communication, the main ground invoked by the Respondent State is that the Complainant's allegations are unfounded because the Algerian justice system did its duty properly. The Respondent State maintains that the examining magistrate and the Indictment Chamber conducted their investigations and worked on all leads, in accordance with their respective mandates, in strict compliance with national criminal procedures, to help bring out the truth. The State considers that it has discharged all the duties that were required in such circumstances.

Concerning Ordinance No. 06-01, the Respondent State maintains that the Complainant's invocation of this document is unfounded insofar as the court's decision was based on facts, hearings of the persons implicated and of witnesses, confrontations and other means of investigation aimed at shedding light on this disappearance. According to the Respondent State, the said Ordinance never served as a basis for the decisions of the two investigating courts in the handling of the Benidir case.

The Respondent State explains that the Complainant cannot invoke the Charter for Peace and National Reconciliation and its implementing texts to exempt himself from not having initiated the available judicial proceedings, constituting local remedies, inciting the Commission to share his suspicion and his preconceptions about the foundations of Algerian justice and the independence of the Judge.

The Respondent State considers the complainant's argument as eminently subjective and politically motivated, and this in his systematic approach of calling into question Algerian justice and the option of reconciliation adopted by the Algerian people in its immense majority.

The Respondent State therefore requests the Commission to find that: the present case was the subject of judicial treatment, in accordance with the procedures in force; the court based itself on facts that were brought to its knowledge and on the judicial investigation that followed to form a conviction and render its decisions; Ordinance No. 06-01 was never invoked by the court; the Algerian State has committed none of the alleged violations.

In response to the Respondent State's observations on the admissibility of the communication, the Complainant takes note of the observations of the Algerian State. He wishes, however, to emphasise that the Respondent State's observations are identical to those already raised at the admissibility stage of the Communication in its earlier briefs and in view of which the Commission has already ruled on the admissibility of the communication. The Complainant deplores that despite the Commission's decision on admissibility, the Respondent State continues to contest the said decision, endlessly delaying the examination of the communication on the merits. He therefore requests the Commission to disregard the State's arguments; to reject its request for inadmissibility and to rule on the merits of the Benidir communication.

In response to the Respondent State's observations on the merits, the Complainant refutes the Respondent State's assertions according to which investigations were conducted by the examining magistrate or the indictment chamber to help bring out the truth about the disappearance of Ali Benidir. The Complainant reiterates that at the end of more than ten years of proceedings, the various complaints of Mr and Mrs Benidir to the different authorities led only to non-suits, referrals, or dismissals without further action, thus calling into question the seriousness of the various investigations conducted in this case. The fate of Ali Benidir has thus still not been clarified. As for the patriots who were formally named by two eyewitnesses as being the perpetrators of the arrest of Benidir which was followed by his enforced disappearance, they were never troubled by Algerian justice for these facts.

Furthermore, the Complainant indicates that Ali Benidir's mother is in no way driven by political motivations and is in no way engaging in "a flagrant abusive misuse of procedure", but simply wishes to find her son. On the contrary, she seized the Algerian courts with her late husband so that an effective and impartial investigation would be conducted and prosecutions brought against those responsible. Ali Benidir's parents therefore cooperated fully with the Algerian authorities and Mrs Houria Berkane wishes more than anything that the Algerian authorities do everything that is legally possible to discover the truth about the fate of her son.

The Complainant also refutes the Respondent State's argument according to which the Algerian judicial authorities never invoked Ordinance No. 06-01. Indeed, the CFDA wishes to recall that Mahmoud Benidir was summoned on 13 March 2007 by the deputy attorney general of the Hussein Dey Court. In the minutes of this summons, the latter explicitly requests the father: "to apply the procedure cited by Ordinance No. 06-01". On the objection of inadmissibility for non-exhaustion of local remedies, lis pendens and the standing of the Complainant to act on behalf of the victims.

On the objection raised by the Respondent State concerning the inadmissibility of the Communication, the Commission considers that there is no need to resume the analysis on admissibility insofar as it has already declared the Communication admissible and rejected the motion for review. These two decisions are therefore authoritative and form the procedural basis of the proceedings on the merits in the context of which the Respondent State has submitted its conclusions.

As for the examination on the merits, the Commission will determine on the basis of the facts and arguments submitted by the parties whether Articles 1, 4, 5, 6, 7(1) and 9(2) of the African Charter have been violated.

On these grounds, the Commission refers to its jurisprudence in Working Group on Strategic Litigation v. Democratic Republic of Congo to recall that its mandate specifically covers the rights contained in the Charter. By virtue of the provisions of Article 60 of the Charter, the Commission may however draw inspiration from principles included in other human rights conventions without however extending the scope of its material jurisdiction to the said instruments. Where appropriate, a link must be established between these principles and those contained in the Charter.

In the present case, the Commission notes that the Complainant does not demonstrate such a link. Moreover, considering that the rights protected by the provisions of the said instruments are usefully guaranteed by the Charter, there is no need to draw inspiration from them.

In sum, regarding the allegations of violation of instruments other than the Charter, the Commission decides, in view of the foregoing, to set them aside from the examination on the merits. The said examination will, consequently, be limited to the allegations of violation of the provisions of Articles 1, 4, 5, 6, 7(1) and 9(2) of the Charter.

Under Article 1 of the African Charter, States parties recognise the rights, duties and freedoms enshrined in this charter and undertake to adopt legislative or other measures to give effect to them. A State's failure to perform its obligation under Article 1 of the Charter may open the way to the violation of substantive rights or at least limit their enjoyment. In this regard, the Commission refers to its jurisprudence to note that, in principle, non-observance of the obligation prescribed in Article 1 is constituted once a violation of a provision of the Charter is found. It follows that any allegation of violation of Article 1 of the African Charter must be supported by proof of the disregard of another substantive right guaranteed by the Charter. The Commission will therefore examine, prior to the determination of a possible violation of Article 1, the allegations of violation of the substantive rights guaranteed by Articles 4, 5, 6, 7(1) and 9(2) of the African Charter.

Article 4 of the African Charter provides that "Human beings are inviolable. Every human being shall be entitled to respect for his life and the integrity of his person. No one may be arbitrarily deprived of this right". Under the violations of the right to life thus guaranteed by the African Charter, the Complainant cites the enforced disappearance of Mr Benidir Ali since his arrest of 29 August 1996.

The terms "enforced disappearances" not being defined by the African Charter, the analysis will be conducted in light of other international rules in accordance with Article 61 of the African Charter in order to determine the definition. The most specific instrument in the matter is the International Convention for the Protection of All Persons from Enforced Disappearance of 20 December 2006.

Under the provisions of Article 2 of the said Convention, "enforced disappearance" is considered to be the arrest, detention, abduction or any other form of deprivation of liberty by agents of the State or by persons or groups of persons acting with the authorization, support or acquiescence of the State, followed by a refusal to acknowledge the deprivation of liberty or by concealment of the fate or whereabouts of the disappeared person, which place such a person outside the protection of the law.

The Commission notes that Mr Ali Benidir disappeared after his arrest on 29 August 1996 by Lahcene Aliche, Mohamed Mayouf, Mustapha Koumina, Nacer Meslem, Makhlouf Barkat and Samir Dandani, all members of the pro-government militia of the Aïn Naadja neighbourhood known by the nickname of "patriots". That the patriots carried out abductions or rackets, and that anyone refusing to collaborate with them became an enemy, an Islamist and therefore a terrorist. It also notes that at the end of more than seventeen years of proceedings, the fate of Ali BENIDIR has still not been clarified and that he allegedly lost his life in incommunicado detention. The Respondent State provides no denial of the facts as reported by the Complainant.

The Commission further notes that after the arrest of Benidir by the patriots, he was taken directly to the car park of the Aïn Naadja Town Hall as maintained by the Complainant. The Commission thus considers that the constituent element of the beginning of the enforced disappearance, namely the deprivation of liberty, is present in the present case. Moreover, from what the evidence establishes, Benidir's relatives have always insistently sought to know the truth about what happened to him, without ever obtaining an answer. The Commission deduces that the arrest, the ignorance of the place of detention and the lack of information on the fate and situation of the victim are constituent elements of an enforced disappearance with regard to Benidir.

The question that arises is whether the enforced disappearance of Benidir must be attributed to the Respondent State as maintained by the Complainant. The Commission notes that the patriots operated if not with the authorisation at least with the consent of the Respondent State. This is notably attested by the fact that the patriots carried out arrests in broad daylight without being troubled. What is more, they had barracks and a headquarters in a car park of the Aïn Naadja Town Hall. This use of a public place - the car park of a town hall - by the patriots to coordinate their activities without being troubled by the authorities is proof of the authorisation or even the acquiescence of the Respondent State to use these public places and to exercise police functions in the Aïn Naadja neighbourhood.

On the basis of this acquiescence, the arrest of Mr Ali Benidir, his detention in an unknown place and his enforced disappearance are attributable to the Respondent State. Even supposing that the patriots escaped the control of State authority, the State's responsibility would remain engaged nonetheless. This is so because Article 1 of the Charter requires States parties to adopt all appropriate measures to ensure the effective protection of the rights of all individuals within their territory and subject to their sovereignty. The undertaking of States parties to give effect to the rights guaranteed by the Charter includes not only that of respecting them, by not themselves infringing them, but also that of protecting them, which includes protection against any infringement to which they might be subject at the hands of non-State actors.

The Commission refers to its decision in Communication 389/12 - Geneviève Mbiankeu v. Cameroon in which it concluded that under Article 1 of the Charter, States are bound not only by the obligation to respect the rights of their citizens but also to protect them against violation by third parties. In accordance with the Commission's jurisprudence, if a State neglects to ensure respect for the rights contained in the African Charter, this constitutes a violation of the said Charter, even when that State or its agents are not the direct perpetrators of this violation. The Commission has also considered that human rights standards do not only contain limits on State power or on State organs. They also impose positive obligations on States to prevent and punish human rights violations committed by private actors. Indeed, human rights oblige States to protect citizens or persons within their jurisdiction against the harmful acts of third parties. Thus, an act perpetrated by a private person, and therefore not directly attributable to a State, may give rise to the responsibility of the State, not because of the act itself, but because of the lack of due diligence to prevent the violation or the failure to take the necessary measures to grant reparation to the victims.

The African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Court) reached the same conclusion in its decision in the case African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights v. Libya (Saif Al Islam Kadhafi Case). In the opinion of the African Court, the State is responsible for its actions as much as for its omissions and indeed has the obligation to adopt measures to ensure, on its territory, the application of the rights guaranteed under the African Charter. Likewise, the European Court of Human Rights ruled more extensively on the question of the positive obligation, concluding in the case Osmanoglu v. Turkey that the State must not only refrain from intentionally and unlawfully causing death, but also has the obligation to take the necessary measures to protect the life of persons within its jurisdiction. In the Case Kaya v. Turkey, the Court concluded that if the evidence was not sufficient to conclude beyond reasonable doubt that Dr Kaya had been killed by State agents, it nevertheless considered that the Turkish authorities had failed in their obligation to take reasonable measures to protect him against a real risk to his life.

The Commission notes that in the present case, Mr Benidir was allegedly arrested by the Patriots who exercised the role of police in public places without being troubled and that the State did nothing to prevent and stop the violation. It therefore concludes that the Respondent State is responsible for the disappearance of Mr Benidir.

Having concluded that the Respondent State is responsible for Benidir's disappearance, the Commission will then determine whether a disappearance can be considered an infringement of the right to life as alleged by the Complainant. To answer this question, the Commission will refer to the jurisprudence of other international courts, notably the Inter-American Court of Human Rights (the Inter-American Court) which has affirmed that the practice of enforced disappearances frequently involves the secret execution of detainees without any other form of trial, followed by the concealment of the corpse with the aim of erasing all material trace of the crime and of granting impunity to the perpetrators, which is a brutal violation of the right to life.

According to the European Court of Human Rights, the violation of the right to life in the case of a disappearance does not stop at finding the absence of material proof of the death of the person reported missing. Proof of the violation of the right to life stems not from the factual elements of an isolated case, but from relating the facts of the case to the existence or not of an official practice of enforced disappearances.

The Commission recalls to that effect the general situation that prevailed in Algeria in the 1990s, defined as the period of the "national tragedy". It therefore cannot in any way be excluded that the arrest of Benidir by the patriots for his real or supposed membership of the Islamist movement and his disappearance were such as to endanger his life.

The Commission further considers that the passage of time may have a certain bearing on the weight to be given to other indications before it can be concluded that the disappeared person may be presumed dead. It must be accepted that the more time passes without any news of the detained person, the more likely it is that he is dead. In this regard, the length of time elapsed since the arrest of Benidir is a factor to be taken into account. The Commission notes that more than 20 years have elapsed without it being possible to obtain information on the fate of Benidir Ali.

Moreover, the Commission, basing itself on the Respondent State's submissions, including notably a fact sheet drawn up by the services of the Ministry of the Interior and Local Authorities which acknowledges that the disappeared person was declared deceased, a victim of the national tragedy, accepts that Benidir is no longer of this world.

In these circumstances, the Commission is of the view that the Respondent State failed in its obligation to protect Mr Benidir Ali against enforced disappearance followed by the loss of his life and is consequently responsible for the violation of Article 4 of the African Charter.

Article 5 of the Charter provides that "Every individual shall have the right to the respect of the dignity inherent in a human being and to the recognition of his legal status. All forms of exploitation and degradation of man particularly slavery, slave trade, torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment and treatment shall be prohibited".

The Commission notes that the Complainant alleges that the Respondent State failed in its obligation to protect Ali Benidir against physical torture and cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment as well as his family against moral torture following the disappearance of their relative. On this precise point, the Respondent State, in its arguments, did not provide proof of the diligence undertaken to protect the victim.
The Commission notes that the present Communication raises questions relating to torture, to the recognition of legal status and to cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment.

In its jurisprudence on torture and inhuman treatment, the Commission adopts the definition of the United Nations Committee against Torture which observes that the distinction between inhuman treatment and torture is to be sought in the nature, purpose and severity of the treatment inflicted. With particular regard to torture, the Committee emphasises, in its General Comment No. 20, that the acts in question must cause excruciating suffering intentionally inflicted, have the purpose of obtaining information or confessions, of punishing the victim for real or supposed acts and be attributable to a State agent or a person acting in that capacity. The Commission adopts this nomenclature in its decision Sudan Human Rights Organisation and Centre on Housing Rights and Evictions (COHRE) v. Sudan.

The Commission notes that according to the facts not contested by the Respondent State, while he was detained at the Aïn Naadja gendarmerie following his first arrest in April 1995, Mr Benidir was subjected notably to the rag torture, beating with truncheons, his genitals tied with a wire to prevent him from urinating, detention in a cell devoid of everything, flooded with water, where he had to sleep on the bare floor, naked and without a blanket.

The Commission considers that the absence of denial by the Respondent State of the facts as reported by the Complainant amounts to acquiescence, the proceedings having been adversarial. This position is consistent with the Commission's constant jurisprudence according to which "where allegations of human rights abuse go uncontested by the Respondent State, ... the Commission must decide on the facts provided by the Complainant and treat those facts as given...".

The Commission notes that these acts caused serious physical and mental suffering to the victim. It finds that these acts were intentionally inflicted by public officials (soldiers of the Aïn Naadja gendarmerie) to punish the victim and obtain information about his supposed or real links with the FIS. In these circumstances, the Commission concludes that acts of torture were committed on the person of Benidir.

Regarding the other alleged violations of Article 5, the Complainant reports acts of torture suffered by Benidir during his second arrest by the patriots in August 1996, notably arbitrary arrest, incommunicado detention without allowing him any contact with his family as well as the enforced disappearance that followed.

The Commission recalls that to be characterised as torture, the acts perpetrated must not only be severe pain or suffering, but above all caused by or at the instigation of a public authority, with the purpose of punishing or of obtaining information or a confession; the said pain or suffering being able to be physical or mental. The notable difference between torture and treatment liable to be assimilated to it is therefore to be sought in the capacity of the perpetrators.

In the present case, the perpetrators were private persons acting in public places and under the authorisation of public authority but without the official capacity of public officials. The Commission considers that even if the Victim suffered acts of a certain severity which caused him both physical and mental suffering, the perpetrators were private persons, "the patriots". Given the official capacity of the perpetrators as a necessary condition for the characterisation of certain acts as amounting to torture, in the present case, there is no need to conclude that there was torture but rather cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment.

On the allegation of the violation of the right to respect for human dignity and of the right to recognition of legal status, in its relevant jurisprudence, the Commission has established a connection of principle between torture, inhuman and degrading treatment and human dignity. This is so, among others, in the cases Modise v. Botswana and Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights and Interights v. Egypt where the Commission considers that inhuman and degrading treatment necessarily violates human dignity.

The Commission has also concluded that all enforced disappearances violate a wide range of human rights, notably the right to security and dignity of the person, the right not to be subjected to torture or to any other cruel, inhuman or degrading punishment or treatment, the right to humane conditions of detention, the right to a legal personality, the right to a fair trial, the right to family life and, when the disappeared person has been killed, the right to life.

This position is consistent with the relevant international jurisprudence which considers that the enforced disappearance of persons constitutes a multiple violation which begins with a deprivation of liberty. The Inter-American Court concluded that enforced disappearance also entails an infringement of the right to recognition of legal personality enshrined in Article 3 of the American Convention, given that the disappearance of a person seeks not only to employ one of the most serious forms of removal of a person from any legal order, but also to deny his existence and to leave him in a situation of legal uncertainty before society and the State.

In all logic, enforced disappearance also violates human dignity and the recognition of legal status. It is therefore appropriate to conclude that these rights have been violated with regard to Ali Benidir.

Regarding the violation of Article 5 of the Charter with respect to Benidir's close relatives, the Complainant alleges that Ali Benidir's wife (Boudahane Nadjat), his mother and his daughter also suffered moral torture in that the disappearance of Mr Benidir, since his arrest on 29 August 1996 by the patriots, has caused anguish and distress among his relatives.

The Commission has already recognised that detaining persons without allowing them any contact with their families and refusing to inform the families of the fact and place of detention of these persons constitute inhuman treatment both for the detainee and for his family. The Commission has also established that any act leading to enforced disappearance causes suffering to the victim himself and to his family.

This position is also corroborated by international jurisprudence. In the case Maria del Calmen de Quinteros et al v. Uruguay, the Human Rights Committee established that the anguish and stress caused to a mother by the disappearance of her daughter in conditions where her fate remained unknown constitute a violation of Article 7 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. For its part, the Inter-American Court concluded that an enforced disappearance constitutes cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment of the victim's family in the same way as of the victim himself. It also recognised that the anguish, suffering, frustration and helplessness of a relative of the victim vis-à-vis the authorities constitute cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment. In the present case, the Commission notes the anguish and distress that the detention and disappearance of Benidir Ali caused to his relatives.

In light of the foregoing, it is appropriate to conclude that the Respondent State violated Article 5 of the Charter, notably the right not to be subjected to torture and to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment with regard to Mr Benidir as well as with regard to his mother and his relatives.

Under Article 6 of the African Charter "Every individual shall have the right to liberty and to the security of his person. No one may be deprived of his freedom except for reasons and conditions previously laid down by law. In particular, no one may be arbitrarily arrested or detained". The Commission recalled the importance of these provisions in the Guidelines on the Conditions of Arrest, Police Custody and Pre-Trial Detention in Africa which prescribe that no one must be deprived of his liberty except on the grounds and according to the procedures laid down by law.

The Commission notes the Complainant's allegation according to which Mr Benidir was subjected to an arrest resembling an abduction for the first time and then a second time in a secret place for his supposed links with the FIS, which constitutes arbitrary detention. It is for the Commission to determine whether the victim's detention is arbitrary.

The Commission has observed that not all actions limiting the physical liberty of an individual constitute a deprivation of liberty under Article 6 of the Charter. But a deprivation of liberty that does not fall within the strict limits of the law or is for unacceptable or simply arbitrary reasons constitutes a violation of Article 6 of the Charter.
In Liesbeth Zegveld and Mussie Ephrem v. Eritrea, the Commission adopted the position that incommunicado detention constitutes a serious violation of human rights under Article 6 of the Charter.

From the Complainant's submissions, the Commission notes that Ali Benidir's first arrest was carried out in a brutal manner. Nothing reveals that his captors informed him of the reason for his arrest, let alone showed him a legal title justifying his arrest. The subsequent detention in a secret place and without contact with his family is testimony that the deprivation of liberty was carried out in violation of Article 6 of the African Charter.
The Commission considers that Benidir's detention is arbitrary. It is consequently appropriate to conclude that the provisions of Article 6 of the Charter have been violated.

Article 7(1) of the African Charter guarantees the right to have one's cause heard under the conditions of a fair procedure. Under the violation of the right to a fair trial, the Complainant alleges that Mr Benidir's family seized all the competent authorities of the Respondent State and exhausted all local remedies without obtaining satisfactory results. On the basis of the Complainant's arguments, the Commission considers that the examination of a fundamental right, the right to an effective remedy (Article 7(1)(a)), should be retained.

The Commission has considered that "the right to justice entails the obligation for the State to investigate violations, to prosecute their perpetrators and, if their guilt is established, to punish them".

The question that arises in the present case is therefore whether the Respondent State fully discharged its obligation and whether it acted with all due diligence. From the outset, it must be acknowledged that the Respondent State took a series of steps with a view to identifying the perpetrators of the abduction of Mr Benidir, notably by investigating the file and hearing the various persons involved in the case.

However, the examination of the file shows that there were a number of failings in the handling of this case by the national courts, notably the absence of prosecution of the 5 militia members alleged to be the perpetrators of the abduction of Mr Benidir and the length of time taken by the national courts to deal with the case.

The Commission considers that the circumstances of the abduction show that "the patriots" operated in public places and were never troubled by the police. The organisation and mode of operation in places known to the police authorities and with their acquiescence constitute, in the Commission's view, sufficient indications that the Respondent State had every latitude to identify the perpetrators of the enforced disappearance of Ali Benidir. However, no proof was provided by the Respondent State that serious investigations were conducted to shed light on the circumstances and the perpetrators of the abduction, as well as the place of detention or the fate of Ali Benidir.
