Sur le volet économique, le Plaignant allègue que le fait d'avoir été empêché de percevoir ses dividendes pendant près de vingt ans a résulté en une perte énorme. Il soutient que cette situation a eu un impact sur sa santé.

La Commission note que par ses conclusions introduites en réponse aux observations orales de l'Etat défendeur à l'audience, le Plaignant estime le dommage subi à 500 millions de francs Rwanda au lieu des 200 millions initialement requis. Pour ce qui est des montants des sommes d'argent objet du contentieux devant les juridictions internes, ils sont clairement évalués par les documents versés au dossier et référencés par les décisions de justice citées. En ce qui concerne les dommages et intérêts requis, la Commission note que le Plaignant n'a malheureusement pas fait la preuve de ce que le montant demandé correspond aux préjudices soufferts. Les montants requis aux différentes étapes de la procédure diffèrent en outre et ne sont pas répartis par préjudice.

L'évaluation du quantum va donc se faire sur une base forfaitaire, puisque les restitutions des montants initiaux vont remettre le Plaignant dans le restitutio in integrum. En tout état de cause, la réparation en droits de l'homme n'a pas nécessairement pour but de punir l'Etat mais de rétablir le Plaignant dans ses droits et d'éviter la survenance de nouvelles violations. Sur ce point, la Commission est d'avis que les violations constatées ont nécessairement eu un impact sur les activités commerciales et professionnelles du Plaignant et que les procédures devant les juridictions internes lui ont coûté aussi bien du temps que des ressources financières. Il y a en outre un certain préjudice moral associé au préjudice professionnel puisque la preuve a été fournie de la connaissance par le public de l'inscription du Plaignant sur la liste des débiteurs insolvables. En revanche, le Plaignant n'a pas suffisamment prouvé l'impact sur sa santé. La Commission,Par ces motifs,

Déclare que la République du Rwanda a violé les dispositions des articles 7(1)(a) et 14 de la Charte africaine. En conséquence : i. Demande à la République du Rwanda de restituer au Plaignant la somme de 4 834 838 francs rwandais. ii. Demande par ailleurs à la République du Rwanda de verser au Plaignant une indemnisation appropriée, juste et adéquate. Le montant de ladite indemnisation sera calculé en prenant en compte les pertes subies du fait du refus de lui accorder de nouveaux crédits, le manque à gagner découlant de l'impossibilité de percevoir les dividendes de ses parts sociales, la perte découlant de l'impact des violations constatées sur ses activités économiques et professionnelles, le temps et les ressources investis dans les procédures internes et les impenses. iii. Demande enfin à la République du Rwanda de lui rapporter par écrit, dans un délai de cent quatre-vingt (180) jours, pour compter de la notification de la présente décision, quant aux mesures entreprises à l'effet de la mise en œuvre de ces recommandations. Adoptée le 17 février 2016lors de la 19 Session extraordinaire de la Commission Africaine des Droits de l'Homme et des Peuples tenue du 16 au 25 février 2016 à Banjul, Gambie.

On 9 November 2010, the Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Secretariat) received from Maître Théogène Muhayeyezu, a Rwandan national, a Complaint submitted pursuant to Article 55 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter). The Complainant is a lawyer at the Bar of Rwanda.
The Communication was submitted against the Republic of Rwanda (a State Party to the African Charter and hereinafter referred to as Rwanda).

The Complainant states that in the course of 1994, the company BP-FINA granted him a credit with a total value of 7,867,939 Rwandan francs representing petroleum products worth 6,922,253 francs and transport costs estimated at 945,686 francs. According to the Complainant, this credit was to be repaid after the sale of the fuel, by means of bank transfers to an account opened by the company BP-FINA at the Banque Commerciale du Rwanda (BCR).

In performance of this undertaking, the Complainant reports having paid into the said account an amount of 5,402,615 francs but that, taking advantage of his absence from Rwanda in 1996, the company BP-FINA and the BCR increased the amount of his debt by unduly debiting the above-mentioned bank account. The Complainant thus states that on 26 September 1996 the company BP-FINA signed a contract with his associates under which the company SOPEGI, of which he is a member, was to reimburse BP-FINA an amount of 4,850,779 francs.

In addition, on 1 January 1997, the company BP-FINA allegedly had the BCR hand over to it an amount of 2,000,000 francs upon presentation of an expired and unfunded cheque that the Complainant had given to his creditor in 1994 as a guarantee of repayment of the credit granted.

In all, the Complainant continues, the company BP-FINA allegedly had a sum of 12,702,777 francs paid to it whereas the debt was only 7,867,939 francs. The Complainant therefore denounces this overpayment in the amount of 4,834,838 francs and reports that, by agreeing to pay the unfunded cheque deposited as a guarantee, the BCR used this pretext to debit his account and place him on the list of insolvent clients.

As a result of these events, the Complainant states that, having undertaken to have his rights restored, he had recourse to the judicial bodies of Rwanda without success. He reports in this regard that of the five applications submitted to the judges none succeeded, the subsequent decisions being riddled with contradictions and others characterised by a lack of reasoning. By way of illustration, the Complainant cites the judgment R.Com AA 0007/09/CS delivered by the Supreme Court of Rwanda on 9 July 2010, by which the Court, while considering the facts as set out, nevertheless refused to answer the questions raised. According to the Complainant, the Court's position would be in violation of Article 141 of the Constitution and Article 147 of the Code of Civil, Commercial, Social and Administrative Procedure of Rwanda.

The Complainant submits that the Supreme Court of Rwanda gave the same treatment to the statements of the witness Emmanuel Mureramanzi cited in the Court's judgment cited above. According to those statements, in agreeing to pay the amount of 4,850,779 francs, the Complainant's associates were not aware of the cheque of 2,000,000 francs deposited as a guarantee. The Complainant considers in this regard that the Supreme Court should have found that the company BP-FINA was reimbursed an amount far greater than the debt it held against him and that he was entitled to the recovery of what was not due under the provisions of Articles 133 and 252 of Book III of the Civil Code of Rwanda (CCL III).

With regard to the same judicial decision, the Complainant further states that the Rwandan high court refused to find in his favour on the question of his inclusion on the list of debtors of the Banque Commerciale du Rwanda, a decision following which he was sentenced by the lower courts to a fine of 3,000,000 francs. Such a refusal is, to say the least, surprising according to the Complainant since the Supreme Court itself had precisely declared unfounded, as unjustified, the counterclaim of the Banque Commerciale du Rwanda seeking recognition of its claim against the Complainant and the related increases.

The Complainant submits that as a consequence of the foregoing, the Supreme Court being the highest court of the Respondent State, it is evident that his property will be put up for sale to recover the sums awarded by the courts of first instance and confirmed by the Supreme Court.

The Complainant alleges that the facts set out above constitute a violation of the provisions of Articles 7 and 14 of the African Charter. He therefore asks the Commission to require the Respondent State to: (i) Declare that the case was wrongly judged; (ii) Condemn the use by the courts of the Respondent State of insulting language; (iii) Grant material compensation in the amount of two hundred million (200,000,000) Rwandan francs; (iv) Grant moral compensation; and (v) Respect its international commitments by guaranteeing his rights in the SOGEPI.

The Complaint reached the Secretariat on 9 November 2010. During its 48 Ordinary Session held from 10 to 24 November 2010 in Banjul, The Gambia, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Commission) considered the Complaint and decided to be seized of it. On 30 November 2010, the Secretariat accordingly informed the Respondent State of the Complaint, requesting it to submit its written observations on admissibility within three months.

By Letter dated 9 December 2010, the Secretariat informed the Complainant that the Commission had decided to be seized of the Complaint and that it intended to decide on admissibility during its 49 Ordinary Session scheduled to be held from 28 April to 12 May 2011 at a venue to be determined. The Complainant was invited at the same time to transmit his arguments on admissibility within one month.

During its 49 Ordinary Session, in the absence of submissions by the parties, the Commission decided to defer consideration of the Communication to its 50 Ordinary Session. On 2 June 2011, the Secretariat informed the parties of this decision and granted them a further period of two months to file their briefs on admissibility.

On 24 June 2011, in response to the Secretariat's correspondence, the Complainant recalled that he had submitted his arguments on admissibility when seizing the Commission and that those arguments should be taken into account in the consideration of the Communication.

During its 50 Ordinary Session held from 24 October to 5 November 2011 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission decided on a further deferral. The parties were informed of this decision and the Secretariat reminded them to submit their arguments on admissibility.

In several pieces of correspondence sent to the Secretariat during July and August 2011, the Complainant recalled once again that he had already submitted his arguments on admissibility and also provided additional information.

On 28 June 2012, the Secretariat informed the parties that during its 51 Ordinary Session held from 18 April to 2 May 2012 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission had considered the Communication and decided to take a decision on admissibility during its 52 Ordinary Session scheduled to be held from 9 to 22 October 2012 in Yamoussoukro, Côte d'Ivoire. A further period of two months was granted to the parties to submit their arguments on the admissibility of the Communication.

On 21 August 2012, the Secretariat sent a reminder Note Verbale to the Respondent State, granting it a final period of two months to submit its arguments on the admissibility of the Communication and indicating that, after this period, the Commission would be obliged to take a decision on the basis of the elements in its possession. The Complainant's observations on admissibility were transmitted to the State at the same time.

On 8 November 2012, the Secretariat received the Respondent State's statement in defence and acknowledged receipt by Note Verbale of the same date. The said statement was transmitted to the Complainant on 9 November 2012. A period of one month was granted to the latter to submit his response.

On 21 January 2013, the Secretariat received from the Complainant an email transmitting his observations on the Respondent State's statement. This transmission brought the exchange of written submissions on admissibility to an end.

During its 53 Ordinary Session held from 9 to 23 April 2013, in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission considered the Communication and decided to defer its decision on admissibility to allow the Secretariat to prepare a draft decision. The Parties were duly informed of this decision.

During its 14 Extraordinary Session held from 20 to 24 July 2013 in Nairobi, Kenya, the Commission considered the Communication and declared it admissible. On 12 August 2013, the Secretariat informed the Parties thereof and requested the Complainant to submit his arguments on the merits within two months of notification of the decision on admissibility.

On 6 September 2013, the Complainant transmitted his observations on the merits. The Secretariat acknowledged receipt on 14 November 2014 and transmitted the said observations to the Respondent State on the same date for the submission of its statement in defence within two months of notification. On 21 January 2014, the Secretariat received the Respondent State's observations, acknowledged receipt and transmitted them to the Complainant on 27 January 2014. The Complainant did not submit a rejoinder at the end of the one-month period granted to him for that purpose.

During its 15 Extraordinary Session held from 7 to 14 March 2014 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission deferred consideration of the Communication to its next session to allow the finalisation of the draft decision on the merits.

On 15 April 2014, the Respondent State seized the Commission with a request for a hearing for the purposes of clarification and the presentation of new or additional information on the merits. During its 55 Ordinary Session held from 28 April to 12 May 2014, in Luanda, Angola, the Commission considered the request for a hearing and decided to require the Respondent State to submit its arguments in writing to enable it to judge the merits of a hearing.

On 22 May 2014, the Secretariat sent correspondence to the Respondent State in this regard. At the end of the period granted to it to submit its arguments, the Respondent State made no response to the Commission's measures of inquiry.
During its 16 Extraordinary Session held from 20 to 29 July 2014 in Kigali, Rwanda, the Commission considered the Communication and rendered a decision on the merits.

On 29 September 2014, the Secretariat received from the Respondent State its arguments relating to the request for a hearing. Having examined the said arguments, the Commission considered that, in order to guarantee a just and fair procedure, the request should be granted. The Parties were informed thereof on 16 March 2015.

On 13 May 2015, the Secretariat informed the Parties that the hearing would be held during the 18 Extraordinary Session of the Commission. On 24 July 2015, the Secretariat informed the Parties that the hearing would be held on 3 August 2015.

On the said date and at the said venue, the Commission heard the Parties. The Secretariat received additional observations by subsequent correspondence. The Parties having been heard and all the observations examined, the Commission rendered its decision.

The Complainant considers that the Communication fulfils all the conditions required by Article 56 of the African Charter to be declared admissible. Focusing in particular on the conditions whose fulfilment is contested by the Respondent State, the Complainant endeavours to prove to the Commission that the requirements laid down in Articles 56(3) and 56(5) of the African Charter have indeed been met.

As regards the requirement laid down in Article 56(3) of the African Charter, the Complainant considers that his Complaint contains no disparaging or insulting language directed against the State concerned, its institutions or the African Union. The Complainant thus submits that no such language appears anywhere in his writings and that the mere fact of his denouncing the insulting terms contained in the judgment R. Com 0150/08/HCC of the High Commercial Court of Rwanda cannot be interpreted as constituting disparaging language within the meaning of the provisions of Article 56(3) of the African Charter.

As regards the condition of exhaustion of local remedies required by Article 56(5) of the African Charter, the Complainant alleges that he has also complied with it. He thus submits that the grievances he formulated were brought before the Supreme Court of Rwanda, the highest court of the Respondent State. While acknowledging the existence and possibility of recourse before bodies such as the Ombudsman and the National Commission for Human Rights (CNDH), the Complainant maintains that such remedies are non-judicial and cannot therefore be regarded as remedies whose exhaustion is required for the admissibility of a communication before the Commission.

Emphasising the efforts undertaken to exhaust local remedies, the Complainant finally alleges that more than seven (7) judicial decisions were rendered by various national courts on the dispute in question. He maintains that such a number of judicial decisions is enough to understand that he can expect nothing from the justice of his country.

The State of Rwanda does not contest the facts as set out by the Complainant. The Respondent State considers, however, that the Communication does not fulfil the conditions required to be declared admissible. In this regard, the State of Rwanda submits that the application does not explicitly indicate which provisions of the African Charter have been violated nor who is the author of the said violations.

As regards specifically the requirements laid down in Article 56 of the Charter, the Respondent State considers that the Communication is not in conformity with the provisions of Article 56(3) of the Charter. The State bases this allegation on the claim that in his brief, the Complainant dared to describe the national judges as "good-for-nothings who do not know what they should do" and as "ill-bred ... who use insulting language".

Finally, the State of Rwanda also contests the Complainant's claim to have exhausted local remedies as prescribed by the provisions of Article 56(5) of the Charter. On this point, the Respondent State considers that both the Ombudsman and the National Commission for Human Rights of Rwanda are local remedies that the Complainant could well have attempted to exhaust before seizing the Commission.

With regard to the Office of the Ombudsman, the State alleges that, established and functioning since 2003, the said body is a public institution independent in the exercise of its functions. According to the State's submissions, the Ombudsman has the mandate to combat injustice by receiving complaints from individuals and associations. The same institution may refer the complaints it receives to the courts and public services, the institutions thus seized being required to respond to it. More particularly, the Respondent State alleges that, in its Articles 79 to 86, Organic Law No. 03/2012/OL of 13 June 2012 determining the organisation, functioning and jurisdiction of the Supreme Court confers on the Office of the Ombudsman the power to seize the said Court with an appeal for review against a final judicial decision tainted by injustice.

The Respondent State maintains that the same possibility was open to the Complainant before the National Commission for Human Rights, an independent national institution responsible for examining human rights violations committed on the territory of Rwanda by State organs, persons acting under the cover of the State, organisations and individuals. According to the State of Rwanda, the National Commission for Human Rights is empowered to investigate human rights violations and to seize the competent national courts. The Respondent State alleges that, having had recourse to neither of these two institutions, the Complainant failed to comply with the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies laid down in Article 56(5) of the African Charter. The Respondent State therefore asks the Commission to declare the Communication inadmissible.

This Communication was submitted in accordance with Article 55 of the African Charter, which gives the Commission competence to receive and consider "communications other than those of States Parties". Such communications must, in order to be declared admissible, fulfil the conditions laid down in Article 56 of the African Charter.

As a prelude to examining the arguments invoked by the parties in relation to the requirements of Article 56 of the African Charter, it is important for the Commission to address the Respondent State's claim that this Communication should be declared inadmissible for having failed to indicate the provisions of the Charter whose violation is alleged. In this regard, the Commission notes that, in his brief on admissibility, the Complainant does mention allegations of violation of Articles 7 and 14 of the African Charter. This argument of the Respondent State must therefore be set aside and the admissibility conditions examined on the basis of the requirements of Article 56 of the Charter.

On examination of the facts set out and the arguments invoked by the parties, it appears to the Commission that compliance with the conditions laid down in Article 56 of the African Charter is not in dispute, with the exception of the requirements of Articles 56(2), 56(3) and 56(5) of the Charter. Under the first requirement, a communication, in order to be declared admissible, must be compatible with the Charter of the OAU or with the African Charter. The second condition requires that the communication not contain disparaging or insulting language. As for the third requirement, it stipulates that the Complainant must have exhausted local remedies unless such remedies have been unduly prolonged.

Concerning the first requirement laid down by Article 56(2) of the African Charter, the Commission notes that the Respondent State, in seeking the rejection of this Communication, argues that the Complainant does not indicate the authors of the alleged violations. The Commission notes in this regard that, in interpreting the requirements of Article 56(2) of the Charter, the Communication must be compatible with the Charter of the OAU or the African Charter, that is to say, inter alia, fall within the Commission's field of competence. Relating to the authors of the alleged violations, it appears that it is the Commission's competence ratione personae that is raised here. In other words, the question posed is who may bring a matter before the Commission and, in this instance, who may be brought before the Commission.

The Commission notes in this regard that the Complainant does allege the violation of his rights under the African Charter following the proceedings before the domestic courts, including the Supreme Court of Rwanda, and the decisions rendered by the said courts. The Supreme Court and the other national courts that heard the case being judicial organs of the Rwandan State, the responsibility of the State is presumed. Such responsibility is understood as encompassing both an obligation for the State to respect the rights protected by the African Charter by avoiding being the author of their violation and an obligation to protect them by ensuring that third parties respect the rights concerned.

It is therefore rightly that this Communication cites Rwanda as the Respondent State in conformity with the provisions of Article 56(2) of the African Charter. The Commission concludes that the Communication does identify the authors of the alleged violations and therefore fulfils the requirement laid down by Article 56(2) of the African Charter.

On the second requirement laid down by Article 56(3) of the African Charter, the Respondent State bases its request for rejection of the Communication on the fact that the Complainant's characterisation of the national judges' decision as unjust and his accusing them of resorting to insulting language constitutes an affront to the authorities of the Respondent State. However, the State of Rwanda was unable to produce in its brief tangible proof of the Complainant's use of disparaging language. The State merely described as disparaging the fact that the Complainant considered the decisions of the national courts to be unjust.

In this regard, the Commission notes that it was unable to find in the Complainant's submissions any insulting or disparaging language directed at the State or any of its authorities. In the absence of proof of such language, the Commission cannot grant the Respondent State's request relating to this requirement. The Commission must therefore find that the Communication does comply with the requirement laid down in Article 56(3) of the African Charter.

As regards the third requirement relating to the exhaustion of local remedies, the Complainant alleges that he fulfilled it since the dispute he brought before the national courts was the subject of a decision rendered by the Supreme Court of Rwanda, whose judgments are not subject to appeal. On the contrary, the State of Rwanda maintains that the National Commission for Human Rights constitutes another remedy and, more particularly, that the Office of the Ombudsman has the power to seize the Supreme Court with a motion for review of a final judicial decision. The Respondent State relies on the failure to seize these two institutions to allege that the Complainant did not exhaust local remedies.

The Commission refers to its jurisprudence to recall that even if, in certain cases, the law of the Respondent State provides for access to judicial remedies through administrative-type remedies, the remedies whose exhaustion is required of the Complainant are mainly of a judicial nature. In the present case, the Commission has no doubt that neither the Office of the Ombudsman nor the National Commission for Human Rights of Rwanda constitutes a judicial remedy. They are rather non-contentious remedies. The exhaustion of these two remedies cannot therefore be required of the Complainant when he has already seized the Supreme Court, which rendered a decision not subject to appeal.

In the opinion of the Commission, requiring the Complainant to use the possibility for the Office of the Ombudsman to request review of the decision rendered by the Supreme Court would be both unrealistic and superfluous. In this instance, the Commission considers that such a possibility of requesting review should rather be understood as applying to the decisions of lower courts that are subject to appeal before the highest court of the State, the Supreme Court. This is all the more so since the texts establishing the Ombudsman and the National Commission for Human Rights were necessarily adopted in conformity with the Constitution of Rwanda (2003), the provisions of Article 144 of which enshrine the supremacy of the decisions of the Supreme Court and stipulate that they are not subject to any appeal except in the case of pardon or review.

Moreover, the Constitution of Rwanda does not cite either of these two institutions as courts or bodies vested with judicial power. As regards the Ombudsman in particular, the Commission notes that the provisions of Article 182 of the Constitution of Rwanda do not establish this body as a court nor confer on it an express power to request the review of decisions of national courts. The said provisions rather provide that "The Office may not interfere in the investigation or trial of cases brought before the courts but may submit the complaints brought before it to the courts or to the services responsible for investigation, which are required to respond to it".

Even supposing that the Complainant had the possibility of requesting review of the Supreme Court's decision through the Ombudsman, such an option is by no means obligatory but merely optional. This is so since, as indicated above, the provisions of Article 56(5) of the African Charter require a complainant to exhaust principally only remedies of a judicial nature.

Moreover, the Commission finds that these two institutions do not constitute remedies whose exhaustion is required for a communication to be declared admissible. Consequently, the Respondent State's argument seeking to have this Communication declared inadmissible for failure to exhaust local remedies cannot succeed.

In light of the foregoing, the Commission finds that the Complainant has exhausted local remedies. Consequently, the Commission concludes that the Communication fulfils the conditions set out in Article 56 of the African Charter.
In view of the foregoing, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights declares this Communication admissible in accordance with Article 56 of the African Charter.

In support of the violation of the provisions of Article 7, the Complainant invokes the misinterpretation of the facts, the failure to refer to legal texts, the refusal to apply the law in force and the lack of reasoning of the decisions rendered by the High Commercial Court of Rwanda. The Complainant alleges in particular that, without indicating the nature of the debt, the said Court admitted the counterclaim of the Banque Commerciale du Rwanda (BCR) and confirmed his inclusion on the bank's list of debtors. Furthermore, the Complainant maintains, the Court rejected all the evidence he presented and demanded specific evidence whereas evidence is free in commercial matters.

The allegations of violation of the provisions of Article 7 also concern the proceedings before the Supreme Court. In this regard, the Complainant alleges a lack of reasoning but also contradictions that he regards as a denial of justice. First, the Complainant maintains that the Supreme Court did not examine the question whether and why the company BP-FINA received an amount greater than that which should have been due to it under their agreement. Furthermore, he points out that while the Court rejects the BCR's counterclaim relating to the increase and the level of the debt arising from the payment of the cheque presented by BP-FINA, the high court refuses to draw the consequence that his name must be removed from the list of debtors. Moreover, the Complainant alleges that the Court's decision confirming its own Judgment R COM AA 0007/08/CS is contradictory. The Complainant finally maintains that the same denial of justice applies to the arguments he invoked before the Supreme Court concerning the payment of the unfunded cheque and the debt that was placed on him without his knowledge.

The Complainant also alleges the violation of the right to property guaranteed in Article 14 of the African Charter. From the first argument invoked in this regard, it emerges that the BCR's refusal to return to him the amount of the initial balance of his personal account prior to the payment of the disputed cheque deprived him of a sum of money constituting his property. In addition, the Complainant invokes in support of the same allegation the fact that the BCR attributed a debt to him by deciding to pay the cheque presented by BP-FINA, which thereby had itself paid an amount far in excess of the sum of money owed. According to the Complainant, it is the refusal of the domestic courts to make these findings and to draw the conclusions therefrom that engages the responsibility of the Respondent State under Article 14 of the Charter.

In general, the Respondent State adopts as its own the reasons and conclusions contained in the decisions rendered by its judicial organs. The State thus alleges that the fact that the domestic courts deliberated in detail on all the questions raised by the Complainant is proof that his rights protected under Article 7 were respected. Rwanda submits that there can be no question of a violation of the provisions of that article because at least seven (07) judicial decisions were rendered by the national courts on the Complainant's various claims.

As regards the allegation of violation of the provisions of Article 14 of the African Charter, the Respondent State maintains that no action or omission alleged by the Complainant is attributable either to Rwanda or to its courts. On the specific question of the refusal to return the balance amount on the Complainant's account, the State recalls that under the provisions of Article 28 of the Decree of 10 December 1951, the cheque is only an instrument of payment on demand and not an instrument of credit. The State further maintains that the Complainant's argument that the payment was made after a long period cannot stand because payment was effective as soon as the cheque was issued. Moreover, the State points out that under the provisions of Article 32(2) of the Decree cited above, if it is not revoked, the cheque may be paid even after the expiry of the time limit and that the BCR was therefore legally justified in paying BP-FINA. The State considers that the delay caused by the war and the fact that the Complainant had issued the cheque in the form of an overdraft for commercial reasons authorised the bank to pay.

On the question of the undue payment, the Respondent State maintains that there is no such thing since the Complainant was unable to provide proof of it before the domestic courts. As for the entry of the Complainant on the BCR's list of debtors on the basis of the credit granted to him without his knowledge, the State notes that the Complainant never contested the balance of his account after the payment of the cheque. The State refers to Article 35 of the Regulation on banking operations to maintain that the balance is deemed correct, not having been contested within thirty (30) days of its communication to the Complainant. The State concludes that the Complainant's inclusion on the list of debtors is merely the logical consequence of the failure to contest the balance and therefore of the payment of the cheque presented by BP-FINA. Finally, the State considers that the domestic courts settled the question of the dissolution of the SOGEPI in an equitable and relevant manner.

The request for a hearing being subsequent to the Commission's decision on admissibility, the questions raised by the Respondent State concerning admissibility must be considered as objections. The main objection raised by the Respondent State concerns the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies. The State reiterates its arguments seeking to demonstrate that the Ombudsman and the CNDH do constitute remedies to be exhausted under Rwandan law. These arguments are based in particular on the contention that these two institutions were indeed capable, under the law, of giving satisfaction to the Complainant.

The Respondent State's oral observations on the merits tended fundamentally to reiterate their initial arguments concerning in particular the violation of the right to property protected under Article 14 of the Charter. According to the Respondent State, the BCR was well founded in paying the cheque issued by the Complainant once the national courts had so decided and the Complainant himself had never contested the account statements sent to him by the bank.

In response to the failure to exhaust local remedies put forward by the Respondent State, the Complainant reiterates his written arguments. The Complainant alleges, without prejudice to the arguments advanced relating to the seizure of the Ombudsman and the CNDH, that he did seize both institutions and produces a copy of correspondence that remained unanswered.

On the merits of the payment of the cheque, in particular in execution of the decisions of the national courts, the Complainant reiterates his written arguments alleging the lack of factual reasoning of the said decisions. As regards the absence of contestation of the account statements, the Complainant maintains that he did contest them but alleges that such contestation is of no importance in this case, the main issue of which is rather the groundless indebtedness imposed on him by the BCR and BP-FINA.

The Commission notes that under the provisions of Rule 107(4) of its Rules of Procedure, "where it has declared a Communication inadmissible, it may reconsider this decision at a later date if it receives a written request from the author, on the basis of new elements". From the wording of these provisions, it emerges that the Commission cannot reconsider its decision when it has declared a Communication admissible.

In the present case, the Respondent State submitted its request for a hearing after the Commission's decision declaring the Communication admissible. The above-cited provisions therefore apply in the present Communication.

Without prejudice to such a conclusion, the Commission considers the Respondent State's oral observations on admissibility. On examination of the related arguments, the Commission notes that, contrary to the requirements under the provisions of its Rules of Procedure cited above, the oral observations made by the Respondent State during the hearing do not reveal "new elements". That said, the said observations provided the Commission with further explanation on the application of the provisions of domestic law. In any event, the Commission reiterates the reasons for its decision on admissibility, which it therefore confirms.
As regards the oral observations of the Parties on the merits, the Commission deliberates on them concurrently with the written observations.

As a preliminary to the examination of the arguments invoked by the Parties on this point, the Commission is of the view that, in order to be established, the alleged violation must, as the Respondent State maintains, be attributable to it. In this regard, the Commission notes that the actions of the organs of the Respondent State are attributable to it, the State being a unitary entity in international law. Furthermore, the obligations of the State under the Charter include a responsibility not to violate the rights guaranteed but also to prevent third parties from violating them.

Turning to the examination on the merits as to the violation of Article 7 of the African Charter, the Commission notes that, in alleging the lack of reasoning of the decisions rendered by the courts of the Respondent State, the Complainant seeks to have the violation of the provisions of Article 7(1)(a) of the Charter found. Under these provisions, "Every individual shall have the right to have his cause heard. This comprises: (a) The right to an appeal to competent national organs against acts violating his fundamental rights as recognized and guaranteed by conventions, laws, regulations and customs in force".

In its Principles and Guidelines on the Right to a Fair Trial and Legal Assistance in Africa, the Commission retains "the guarantee of a decision rendered without undue delay, notified in a timely manner and reasoned" as an essential element of the right to a fair hearing in general. It is noteworthy that none of the sub-provisions of Article 7(1) of the African Charter expressly mentions the right to a reasoned decision. Despite this absence of express mention, the Commission is of the view that such a right is inherent in the provisions concerned, in this instance in the provisions of Article 7(1)(a).

Indeed, even if the Commission has not specifically found a violation of the right to a reasoned decision, it has recognised, for example in Good v. Botswana, that such a right is a component of the right to bring a case before a competent national court under Article 7(1)(a) of the African Charter. Moreover, inter alia in Amnesty International v. Zambia, the Commission recognises the right to appeal as falling within the provisions of Article 7(1)(a). Such a categorisation is consistent with the practice of both the European Court and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, which, in sanctioning the lack of reasoned decisions, found a violation of Articles 6(1) and 8(1) of their respective conventions, whose provisions correspond to those of Article 7(1)(a) of the African Charter.

The right to a reasoned decision being thus anchored in the provisions of Article 7(1)(a) of the Charter, the Commission observes that the requirement for the judge to elucidate the reasons for the solution he or she gives to a dispute has gone beyond a mere formal requirement to consolidate itself as a substantive principle central to the confidence of litigants in justice and therefore to the very protection of the right to a fair trial. It is therefore indeed a right widely recognised for litigants in both domestic and international systems.

The practice of domestic courts offers relevant and appropriate illustrations of the judge's duty to give reasons for decisions in order to meet the parties' right to a fair trial. Thus, for example in Dibagula v. The State, the Court of Appeal of Tanzania decided that the judge a quo had not respected the right to a fair trial "by simply endorsing the conclusions of the Public Prosecutor without seeking to assess the evidence provided or giving reasons for his decision to adopt the said conclusions. The need for courts to give reasons for their decisions stems from the fact that reasons contribute to clarity and minimise the chances of arbitrariness". The Court of Appeal noted in conclusion that the judge in charge of the case had not only failed to formulate the relevant questions but had also made no attempt to examine those questions.

Regional human rights bodies also recognise the right to a reasoned decision not only in law but also in fact, that is, entailing an obligation on the competent court to carry out an exhaustive, faithful and fair consideration of the facts of the case. This latter aspect of the obligation to give reasons is developed by the European Court of Human Rights in its judgment K.K. v. France, where it condemns the failure of the court to give reasons, notably in fact. To reach this conclusion, the Court notably considered "that while the Applicant had presented a fairly detailed account supported by several documentary exhibits tending to corroborate the facts set out, the trial court dismissed them by means of succinct reasoning". Furthermore, the Court concluded notably in Baucher v. France that a lack of reasoning is liable to violate the right to have one's cause heard where such a lack prevents the parties from deciding in an informed manner whether or not to exercise their right of appeal, and on what grounds.

In light of these jurisprudential developments, the Commission notes that the right to have one's cause heard does include the parties' right to a reasoned decision, in law but also in fact, and that such a right is based on the need to guarantee three fundamental objectives: (i) To constitute a bulwark for the parties against the arbitrariness of the judge, since it gives rise to an obligation for the judge to develop legal reasoning that confronts the law and the facts, thus guaranteeing to litigants that their claims and arguments have been seriously and fairly examined; (ii) To inform the Applicant given that it is the reasoning, in that it informs the parties of the reasons explaining the position adopted by the judge, that will then provide the necessary support for challenging the decision in a rational manner; and (iii) To guarantee and make possible the right to appeal, because the obligation to give reasons calls for submission to review in that the right to reasoning is the preliminary to a right to challenge the decision.

In the present case, the Commission notes that the Complainant alleges both a lack of reasoning and an outright refusal to rule on certain arguments he invoked before the domestic courts. As regards the lack of reasoning, the Commission notes that while it said it could not indicate the nature of the debt imputed to the Complainant, the High Commercial Court admitted the BCR's counterclaim to be reimbursed this debt and to maintain the Complainant on the list of its debtors. Moreover, the proof provided by the Complainant, by means of deposit statements, of the deposit into BP-FINA's account of more than 5 million Rwandan francs was manifestly not taken into account in determining whether there had been an undue payment to the Complainant's detriment.

Concerning the proceedings before the Supreme Court, the Complainant alleges the failure to rule on his arguments relating to the payment of the unfunded cheque and the payment of an undue debt. In particular, on the question of the constitution of the debt induced by the payment of the unfunded cheque, the Commission notes that the Supreme Court merely reiterated the reasoning of the trial court without assessing to what extent that court had relevantly raised and settled, in fact and in law, the questions submitted to it. Such a failing is manifest when the high court rejects the counterclaim for an increase in the debt alleged by the BCR for lack of proof of the initial state of the debt without ruling on the very existence of the debt as examined by the High Commercial Court. The same failing is observed with regard to the payment of the unfunded cheque even though the parties had presented evidence and cited witnesses on both arguments.

On the basis of the legal principles set out above, the Commission finds that, even if the national courts amply examined the questions submitted by the Complainant, the decisions that resulted suffered from a lack of reasoning in fact for some of the arguments invoked but also from a total failure of examination for others. It remains to be seen whether, in the present case, such failings encroached on one of the components identified above of the right protected under Article 7(1)(a). In this regard, the Commission observes that the Complainant's right to be informed of the reasons for the decisions rendered by the domestic courts is a corollary of the right to appeal. This is so since the appellant cannot decide usefully and in an informed manner to appeal if he does not know the reasons for the decision he intends to submit to judicial review. In the present case, the Commission notes that the Complainant was indeed duly informed since he did appeal, notably against the decision of the High Commercial Court, before the Supreme Court. The Complainant's right to appeal, guaranteed in Article 7(1)(a), was therefore respected.

On the other hand, it appears to the Commission that the failings it has noted encroached on the Complainant's right to be protected against the arbitrariness of the judge. In this regard, the Commission finds that the said failings had the consequence of undermining the Complainant's hope of having his cause heard fairly. This consequence is illustrated by the fact that, the Supreme Court's decision being not subject to appeal, the refusal to give reasons for it, the repetition of the reasoning of the trial judge or even the refusal to rule on certain arguments that had nevertheless been invoked, put an end to any hope of having his cause heard. This was so even though the Complainant continued to allege the denial of justice resulting from the decisions of the trial courts and the high court did not rule at all on the fundamental questions relating thereto. It was indeed a denial of justice. In these circumstances, the Commission concludes that the right guaranteed in Article 7(1)(a) of the African Charter was violated.

Under the provisions of Article 14 of the African Charter, "the right to property shall be guaranteed. It may only be encroached upon in the interest of public need or in the general interest of the community and in accordance with the provisions of appropriate laws". In support of the argument based on the violation of these provisions, the Complainant alleges the failure of the domestic courts to find that the BCR refused to return to him the amount constituting the balance of his account before the payment of the unfunded cheque. Furthermore, the Complainant considers that the refusal to rule on the constitution of the debt induced by the payment of the said cheque and on the surplus unduly received by BP-FINA amounts to a violation of the right to recover these sums of money that constitute his property.

The Commission has not defined property or the exhaustive content of the right to property protected under Article 14 of the Charter. The Commission notes, however, that in its ordinary legal meaning, a sum of money does represent property in that it is the object of a subjective right to use, enjoy and dispose of a thing in an exclusive and absolute manner subject only to the restrictions established by law. The sums of money that are the subject of the dispute before the domestic courts do constitute property. It remains to be verified whether they were the property of the Complainant and whether he was deprived of this property without justifiable reason.

In its jurisprudence on the right to property, the Commission has in general found a violation attributable to the Respondent State on the finding of confiscation, seizure or refusal to return property following acts of State authorities or third parties. There have also been cases of eviction, expropriation or destruction. In the present case, it falls to the Commission to determine whether the national courts satisfied the obligation incumbent on the Respondent State to prevent the BCR and BP-FINA from retaining the Complainant's property in the event that it is established.

From the documentary evidence produced by the Complainant, the Commission notes that he was, at the time of the facts, the holder with the BCR of account No 45558, whose balance was in credit in the amount of 101,997 Rwandan francs in 1994. The Complainant had then negotiated with the company BP-FINA and on behalf of the company SOGEPI that he managed, petroleum products for an amount of 7,867,939 francs. By agreement between the parties, repayment of the debt thus granted was to be made by progressive payments into account 46982 opened by BP-FINA at the BCR. SOGEPI being then only at its beginnings, the Complainant had given BP-FINA as a guarantee a cheque in the amount of 2,087,868 francs on his personal account No 45558 mentioned above. The BCR acknowledges having paid this cheque three years later on presentation by BP-FINA although it was not funded and its validity date had expired.

Moreover, the Complainant also produced in the file of this Communication, statements of payments into account No 46982 up to an amount of 5,402,615 francs as repayment of the fuel credit granted to SOGEPI for the operating needs of its petrol station. Finally, BP-FINA had itself paid by the Complainant's associates, in the latter's absence, a sum of 4,850,779 francs as partial payment of the debt of 7,867,939 francs mentioned above.

The Commission notes that the Complainant's right to property over the amount of 101,997 francs constituting the balance of his personal account No 45558 is uncontested by the Parties both in the national proceedings and in the present Communication. Furthermore, the copies of account statements placed in the file are tangible proof thereof. The payment to BP-FINA by the Complainant's associates of the sum of 4,850,779 francs is likewise not contested. Even if this sum of money was paid out of SOGEPI's funds, the Commission notes that, being one of the shareholders of the said Company, the Complainant is entitled to claim a right of property over these funds. Moreover, the Complainant, who managed SOGEPI at the time of the facts and had made alternative payments, held a right of property over any surplus subsequently received in connection with the same debt. The proof of this is that after his return from exile, the Complainant's associates questioned him about the payments that should have been made.

Moreover, the Commission notes that the payment of the unfunded cheque in the amount of 2,087,868 francs induced a debt for which the Complainant was liable and consequently encumbered his property in the form of a sum of money. The Commission will determine later whether the payment is undue and the consequences that must follow therefrom if any. As regards the sums of money in the amount of 5,402,615 francs, they are also manifestly the property of the Complainant since he produces statements indicating that he deposited them into the BP-FINA account opened for that purpose at the BCR. However, although the said statements are contained in the file of the present Communication, the Complainant's right of property over the sum of money concerned is contested by the domestic courts of the Respondent State. The same courts adopted a similar position concerning the Complainant's right over the sum of money constituting the debt induced by the payment of the unfunded cheque. The subsequent examination will consist in determining whether the reasons for such a position conform to legal logic, equity and justice.

Beginning with the payment of the unfunded cheque, the Commission notes that in order to justify it, the High Commercial Court of Rwanda held that even though the said instrument was issued in 1994 it remained valid in 1997 despite its validity date having expired. To so conclude, the trial court considered that the Complainant's failure to revoke the cheque and never having contested the balance statements left the BCR free to pay BP-FINA. According to the Court, the Complainant was in a business relationship with BP-FINA and the BCR was entitled to grant the Complainant an overdraft credit in order to pay the cheque for commercial reasons.

The Commission notes that on the date of presentation by BP-FINA, the Complainant's account showed a balance of 101,997 Rwandan francs and was therefore not sufficiently in credit to honour a cheque in the amount of 2,087,868 francs. Such an operation would of course have been made possible by means of a bank overdraft. However, such a mechanism is governed by very specific rules, including the requirement of a formal and express request from the holder of a bank account. Among other things, it is a universally recognised rule that a bank overdraft may be occasional or temporary, that is to say granted for a limited period of time. In any event, the said facility cannot be granted by the bank to a customer without the express request, without the knowledge and without the consent of the latter. These prerequisites are well confirmed by the conditions required by the BCR itself for the granting of a bank overdraft.

In the present case, the Commission notes that the Complainant never requested or obtained any credit from the BCR and that his account was insufficiently funded to honour the amount of the cheque paid. On the argument that the Complainant would have acquiesced in the payment, the Commission notes that such an argument is not plausible given that the Complainant constantly alleged having already paid the initial debt by payments into BP-FINA's account. Consequently, the Commission finds that the High Commercial Court's considering as compliant with the law and with the BCR's own banking regulations the payment of an unfunded cheque on the basis of a credit to which the Complainant never subscribed enshrines an undue indebtedness. Such indebtedness violates the Complainant's right to property over the sum of money in question.

As regards the sum of money in the amount of 5,402,615 francs paid into BP-FINA's account as payment of the initial debt, the Commission notes that the trial court rejects the Complainant's claims of ownership for lack of proof. In reality, the Court concluded that the statements of payments made by the Complainant into BP-FINA's account were not sufficient to establish payments, still less to demand their recovery. In the Court's understanding, the said statements had to indicate the reasons why the payments were made in order to make it possible to determine whether there had been an overpayment.

The Commission notes that such conclusions enshrine the recognition of evidence produced by the Complainant while the same court rejects the appeal for lack of proof. Evidently, the examination of this argument by the trial court reveals contradictions and does not necessarily follow a certain logical legal analysis. Indeed, the Complainant's associates stated at the bar that they had paid BP-FINA the alternative sum of 4,850,779 francs as payment of the debt of 7,867,939 only because they had never been aware of the cheque of 2,087,868 francs already received by BP-FINA. The Complainant having constantly alleged and proved the payment of an alternative amount of 5,402,615 francs in payment of the same debt, it should have fallen to the trial court to require proof to the contrary from the party contesting the payment.

The Commission notes that the business relations between the Complainants having been established by the trial court, the reasons for any payments of sums of money by the Complainant into BP-FINA's account were presumed. The Commission concludes that the trial court's refusal to establish the payment of the funds concerned in favour of the Complainant for failure to indicate the reasons for payment deprived the Complainant of his right to claim the return of a sum of money that was the property of SOGEPI, for which he was responsible at the time of the facts.

The Commission has already found above that, seized of an appeal against the decision of the High Commercial Court, the Supreme Court of Rwanda simply omitted to rule on the Complainant's arguments relating to the violations alleged in the present Communication. Such an omission could have been justified if the Court's conclusions had settled or rendered moot the ignored arguments. The Commission notes that this is not the case in the present Communication and that, on the contrary, the omitted arguments constituted the anchor point of the dispute brought before the national courts. In these circumstances, the Commission notes that, by ruling as it did, the high court, through a denial of justice, confirmed the violation of the right to property established above.

On the argument relating to the dissolution of SOGEPI, the Commission notes that the Complainant does not sufficiently prove how the judge's refusal to dissolve the Company violates his rights under Articles 7 and 14 of the African Charter. The related request cannot therefore be examined. On the argument relating to the removal of the Complainant's name from the BCR's list of debtors, the Commission is of the view that it will be answered by the consequences flowing from the conclusions relating to the questions settled above.

On the basis of the preceding related developments, the Commission finds that in the present case, the actions of its judicial institutions engage the responsibility of the Respondent State. Furthermore, the acts of private entities, in this instance the BCR and BP-FINA, engage the Respondent State, which failed in its obligation to protect the Complainant against violations committed by third parties.

The requests made by the Complainant were indicated above. The Commission having upheld the Complainant in some of his arguments, the related requests must be examined. In this regard, the Commission notes that its analysis on the merits amply answers the first request. The question of the use of insulting language having been settled at the admissibility stage, there is no need to return to it on the merits. As for the question of the protection of the Complainant's rights in SOGEPI, it was settled above.

On the request for payment of damages, the Commission notes that despite the lack of express mention, the African Charter does guarantee a right to reparation for violations of the rights it protects. The Commission further notes that it has, in general, referred the determination of the quantum of such reparation to the domestic courts of the Respondent State, which are deemed better placed to provide for it, technically and materially. That said, the said courts are implicated in the acts of the Respondent State whose non-conformity with the Charter has just been established. It would therefore be inappropriate to refer the Complainant to the said courts to obtain reparation.

As a result of the foregoing, it falls to the Commission to indicate the form and nature of the reparation that the Respondent State must grant. In this regard, the Commission notes that the Complainant alleges moral and material prejudice. As regards moral prejudice, he alleges that the entry on the list of insolvent debtors had a harmful impact on his public image, in particular as a lawyer. He further considers that this moral prejudice also gave rise to material prejudice reflected in a loss of clientele and therefore a negative impact on his professional activities and the related economic gain. On the economic aspect, the Complainant alleges that having been prevented from receiving his dividends for nearly twenty years resulted in an enormous loss. He maintains that this situation had an impact on his health.

The Commission notes that by his submissions filed in response to the Respondent State's oral observations at the hearing, the Complainant estimates the damage suffered at 500 million Rwandan francs instead of the 200 million initially requested. As regards the amounts of the sums of money that are the subject of the dispute before the domestic courts, they are clearly assessed by the documents placed in the file and referenced by the cited judicial decisions. As regards the damages requested, the Commission notes that the Complainant has unfortunately not proved that the amount requested corresponds to the prejudice suffered. The amounts requested at the different stages of the procedure moreover differ and are not broken down by prejudice.

The assessment of the quantum will therefore be done on a lump-sum basis, since the restitution of the initial amounts will restore the Complainant to restitutio in integrum. In any event, reparation in human rights is not necessarily intended to punish the State but to restore the Complainant to his rights and to avoid the occurrence of new violations. On this point, the Commission is of the view that the violations found necessarily had an impact on the Complainant's commercial and professional activities and that the proceedings before the domestic courts cost him both time and financial resources. There is moreover a certain moral prejudice associated with the professional prejudice since proof was provided of the public's knowledge of the Complainant's entry on the list of insolvent debtors. On the other hand, the Complainant did not sufficiently prove the impact on his health. The Commission, For these reasons,

Declares that the Republic of Rwanda has violated the provisions of Articles 7(1)(a) and 14 of the African Charter. Consequently: i. Requests the Republic of Rwanda to return to the Complainant the sum of 4,834,838 Rwandan francs. ii. Further requests the Republic of Rwanda to pay the Complainant appropriate, just and adequate compensation. The amount of the said compensation shall be calculated taking into account the losses suffered as a result of the refusal to grant him new credits, the loss of earnings arising from the impossibility of receiving the dividends on his shares, the loss arising from the impact of the violations found on his economic and professional activities, the time and resources invested in the domestic proceedings and the expenses incurred. iii. Finally requests the Republic of Rwanda to report to it in writing, within one hundred and eighty (180) days from the notification of this decision, on the measures undertaken to implement these recommendations. Adopted on 17 February 2016 at the 19 Extraordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights held from 16 to 25 February 2016 in Banjul, The Gambia.
